Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women remain a contender in deeper Pac-12 Conference | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
Editor’s note: This is the fifth and final story in a series examining the offseason for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program.

It’s not anywhere close to the original, but for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program the refashioned Pac-12 Conference that it will now call home will present plenty of challenges.

More so than the West Coast Conference – although the Zags’ final season in the WCC was arguably their most entertaining and tightly contested ever.

The WCC has historically been light on competitive depth. Last season was an outlier. Most years two, maybe three teams challenged for league and conference tournament championships.

The respect Gonzaga forged in the WCC will likely follow it into the Pac-12. In way-too-early 2027 NCAA Tournament bracketology, the Zags are picked to earn the automatic bid from the Pac-12.

The Zags are seeded anywhere from No. 7 to No. 10 in early 2027 NCAA Tournament brackets.

Of the nine Pac-12 teams, Gonzaga (24-10), Colorado State (27-8), Oregon State (23-12) and San Diego State (27-6) are expected to jockey for spots in the top four. But Washington State (9-25) and Boise State (25-9) will definitely have a say in how things play out.

San Diego State won the Mountain West regular-season title last year and Colorado State won the conference tournament to earn a bid to the NCAA Tournament.

“The level of play is going to be high and it’s going to be a very competitive conference season,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said.

Fresno State (15-18), Utah State (6-24) and Texas State (11-19) will likely finish in the lower third. Utah State tied for last in the Mountain West last season, and Fresno State and Texas State have new coaches.

“We’re going to get to play each other twice which is not all that common anymore,” Fortier said. “The Power 4 (conferences) don’t do that. And we didn’t do that in the WCC last year. We’ll get a true (regular-season) champion. I’m looking forward to that. We’re going to be pushed every night.”

The conference tournament format will be just like the WCC with the top two seeds receiving double byes to the semifinals and the No. 3 and No. 4 teams getting byes to the quarterfinals.

Of the new teams, Gonzaga is most familiar with Colorado State. The Zags lost in overtime two years ago in Ft. Collins, Colorado, and fell 70-66 at McCarthey Athletic Center last year.

“They’re tough every year,” Fortier said. “They’ve always been a contender to win the Mountain West.”

San Diego State returns four starters and Oregon State returns three from last year and a fourth who started two years ago is back after sitting out following knee surgery.

Washington State returns all of its starters and a sixth who started 20 games.

Based on the final NET rankings from 2025-26, the new fangled Pac-12 will be much stronger than the WCC.

Here were the final NET rankings for the teams that will comprise the Pac-12: Gonzaga (62), SDSU (66), Colorado State (67), OSU (85), Boise State (120), Fresno State (173), WSU (227), Texas State (251).

Here were the final NET rankings for the remaining WCC teams: Santa Clara (80), Loyola Marymount (108), Pepperdine (132), Portland (134), San Francisco (157), Saint Mary’s (183), Pacific (208), San Diego (268) and Seattle U (342). Denver (293) joins the WCC this fall.

Transfer portal, eligibility, recruiting

Gonzaga has had to use the transfer portal to fill roster holes the last two years. But Fortier hopes it will be a supplemental part of recruiting moving forward.

While many programs across the nation are leaning heavily into the transfer portal to sustain or improve, Fortier wants to resist the temptation. Gonzaga has been built on signing high school players and developing them. She doesn’t plan to deter from the formula.

“We’re pretty excited that we can finally do some building,” Fortier said. “It’s really challenging nowadays where you’re just reorganizing and trying to figure out who you have and what they can do with the way the transfer portal has been. It’s been so discombobulated.”

Fortier doesn’t have to harken back too far to recall the most recent team she developed largely through high school signings. The 2023-24 team, which posted the best record in school history (32-4), started five seniors, four in a fifth year who had signed with Gonzaga out of high school. Whether that can happen again remains to be seen.

The recent change in eligibility rules means it could be at least another two years before Gonzaga dips deep into the high school pool.

The new age-based eligibility the NCAA adopted beginning in 2026-27 allows athletes five years of eligibility to be completed within a strict five-year period. Returning players are grandfathered into the new rule and receive an additional year of eligibility unless they’ve already used a redshirt or medical waiver.

Fortier said 11 of 12 players on her roster are eligible for an additional year. The exception is sophomore Lauren Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and medical waiver.

The Zags have four seniors on the 2026-27 roster – Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso, McKynnlie Dalan and incoming transfer Jocelyn Medina. Fortier said she will determine which players want to return for another season at a later date.

Gonzaga has an oral commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Alyah Cornwall for the 2027 recruiting class. At this point Cornwall is the lone commitment for the early signing period in November.

The 5-foot-8 Cornwall is a true point guard – pass first, score second. It’s been a few years since the Zags had a point guard with a quarterback mindset.

Still, Cornwall can score. In 28 games last year at G-Prep, she averaged 17.9 points, 9.9 rebounds, 5.3 assists and 3.3 steals. She was the Greater Spokane League most valuable player and defensive player of the year.

“She loves getting other people involved,” Bullpups coach Geoff Arte said. “But she can really score it too and finishes around the rim. She loves to push the basketball and get it up ahead.”

Fortier said she’s not certain if she’ll sign others. NCAA rules allow schools to have 15 athletes on scholarship. With 12 players Fortier has some options.

Nonconference

Gonzaga will have fewer conference games than it has had in the WCC with just nine teams in the Pac-12.

Additionally, the NCAA expanded the number of games schools can play from 31 to 32. With 16 conference games that means Gonzaga has scheduled 16 nonconference contests.

Gonzaga is finalizing many of its nonconference games including a tournament in Hawaii where the Zags will take on Cal on Nov. 23.

What is known is Gonzaga opens the season at home Nov. 2 against North Dakota State, a return game from a year ago when the Zags opened at NDSU. Nov. 2 is the earliest date any colleges can play this season.

Another announced opponent is Michigan State in a neutral court matchup with the Gonzaga and Michigan State men Dec. 19 in Palm Springs, California.

The Zags will complete a two-year agreement with Arizona State, traveling to Tempe, Arizona, on Dec. 6.

A familiar nonconference opponent returns to the schedule with Montana, which visits Gonzaga Nov. 18. It’ll be an interesting matchup considering the Grizzlies picked up former Gonzaga guard Paige Lofing in the transfer portal this spring.

Those are the known dates at this time. Gonzaga will travel to Stanford and also will play Eastern Washington.

Gonzaga will also have return games at home against UC Riverside and at Grand Canyon.

“I think it’s really going to be a tough (nonconference) schedule,” Fortier said. “We have a couple of really hard games. But I think this team is up for it.”

Another Fortier milestone

Fortier tied LSU coach Kim Mulkey as the fastest coach to reach 300 career victories last season.

Looking back, Fortier said reaching 300 wins didn’t mean much to her.

“I’m just happy for the players and for the (assistant) coaches,” Fortier said. “We care more about how many weddings we get to go to and which babies we get to hold and which players come back. We like to watch them be successful in their life (after basketball).”

Whether she likes it or not, Fortier is closing on another milestone and it’ll happen quickly in the 2026-27 season. Going into her 13th season with her faithful assistants who include her husband Craig, Stacy Clinesmith and Jordan Green – each of whom have been around as long as she has – Lisa Fortier will become Gonzaga’s all-time winningest coach.

She has a 313-84 record (.788 winning percentage). She’s four wins from passing Kelly Graves, who she succeeded. Graves was 316-186 (.699) in 14 seasons.

“I would just say that I’m just grateful to have been part of the building of the program and get us to that place where we were able to just continue and take it to the next level,” Fortier said. “And now I’m ready for us to hopefully take what we’ve done to the next level as well.”

Gonzaga.title: 'Man, it's going to pass.' New Gonzaga wing Chauncey Wiggins navigated summer of uncertainty before earning fifth year
Gonzaga.summary:
Chauncey Wiggins gave Florida State’s upset bid a jolt of life with 37 seconds left during an ACC Tournament quarterfinal game against top-ranked Duke last March.

With the Seminoles trailing 80-77, Wiggins received the ball on the right corner and went to work on Duke’s Cameron Boozer, backing the Naismith Award winner down until he got to his spot outside of the paint. That’s when Wiggins used his long frame to pull up over the sturdy, 6-foot-10 center, and sink a 13-foot step back shot that trimmed the Blue Devils’ lead to one.

The clutch jumper represented the 967th and 968th points of Wiggins’ career – the last ones he’d score as a college basketball player. Or so he thought.

Florida State came out on the wrong end against Duke, losing 80-79, and subsequently turned down an invitation to play in the NIT, signaling the end of Wiggins’ college journey.

The wing was prepared to turn the page, fulfilled with how his four college seasons played out. He made consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances at Clemson, playing key bench minutes for the 2023-24 team that advanced to the Elite Eight. Under first-year Florida State coach Luke Loucks, he averaged double figures for a group that claimed the Seminoles’ first winning ACC record since 2020-21. He nearly eclipsed the 1,000-point milestone, posted a career win-loss record of 92-45 and earned academic honors at Clemson in 2024.

An All-ACC selection would’ve been a nice bonus, but outside of that Wiggins didn’t have too many complaints with his college resume.

“I thought college was over,” Wiggins said. “I thought it was a good four years. Making it to March Madness, that was my dream. I wish I’d gotten on the All-ACC team but I didn’t. I thought my college career was done.”

As Wiggins went through the pre-NBA draft process, there were murmurs that he and other class of 2022 high school graduates might have another shot to play college ball through the NCAA’s new age-based eligibility rules, permitting student-athletes to play five seasons over five years.

Wiggins didn’t think much of it as he traveled for NBA workouts with the Miami Heat, Los Angeles Lakers, Phoenix Suns, Sacramento Kings and Dallas Mavericks, eventually latching on with the Boston Celtics for NBA Summer League in Las Vegas.

“I literally kept telling one of my friends, ‘This thing ain’t going to happen at all, we’re not getting another year,’” Wiggins said. “Then a few weeks after that, our class didn’t get grandfathered in. So we were like, yeah it’s done.”

One friend, former Utah State guard MJ Collins Jr., was insistent, telling Wiggins, “Man, it’s going to pass.”

Not long after he completed his Summer League assignment with the Celtics, Wiggins returned home to Atlanta and began to monitor the college basketball news cycle, eventually learning Collins Jr., new Gonzaga point guard Javon Bennett – a transfer from Dayton – and other players in Ohio had challenged the NCAA in court to secure another year of eligibility.

Wiggins got together with family members, his agent and a lawyer to explore the possibilities, eventually joining a separate group of fifth-year hopefuls seeking a similar injunction in his home state of Georgia.

After finishing a workout on July 31, Wiggins opened up social media and learned about the class-wide injunction in Colorado that granted fifth-year seniors in all sports an extra year of eligibility. Less than a week later, a state judge ruled in favor of Wiggins and other players who filed in Georgia, giving the transfer wing another layer of security.

“So I’m kind of double-protected, if that makes sense,” Wiggins said.

Before either ruling, Wiggins was already hearing from high-major college programs around the country, including Gonzaga, Georgia, SMU, Washington and the Florida State program he recently played for. Wiggins also had pro options on the table, including a G League offer from the Kings and an opportunity with a club team in Japan’s top league.

At Gonzaga, his point of contact was assistant coach RJay Barsh, who worked on Leonard Hamilton’s staff at Florida State in 2022-23. Wiggins and Barsh didn’t overlap in Tallahassee, but the Gonzaga assistant was familiar with the wing’s game from Florida State’s encounters with Clemson in the ACC. It also helped they had a mutual friend in FSU assistant Director of basketball operations Ryan Shnider, a former graduate assistant under Hamilton who stayed on staff when the Seminoles hired Loucks.

“From a basketball standpoint, (Barsh) was recruiting me just saying you’re going to play 2, 3, 4 here,” said Wiggins, who primarily played the 4 and occasionally as small-ball 5 at his last two schools. “Even when he said the 2, I was kind of surprised. … He was like, we’ve got some good length and good guys here. He said we have positions but just say if you get the rebound, you’re going to push the ball and now you have to know what to call. Then obviously coaches can say that and not mean it. Obviously I’m an older guy so I know what I want. Also I had to ask him, can I see some clips of this?”

Shnider also had a relationship with Jalen Warley, who successfully made a similar transition from Florida State to Gonzaga, where he was one of Mark Few’s most valuable two-way players during last year’s 31-win campaign. Wiggins reached out to Warley to get an honest and transparent evaluation of Gonzaga’s program, coaching staff and culture.

“He really loved it there,” Wiggins said. “He really loved it, had a lot to say about the coaches in a positive way. I was like, hey just be realistic. He was like the coaches, what they say is true basically.”

An Atlanta native who’s only resided in Georgia, South Carolina and Florida, Wiggins was familiar with Gonzaga but couldn’t have identified Spokane on a map of Washington. (He admits he originally thought it was a suburb of Seattle). By the time he was born in 2004, the Zags had already planted their flag on the national stage, and Wiggins became accustomed to hearing the school’s name every year, usually whenever March rolled around.

“I watched Gonzaga when I got into college and when I was in high school, but even when I was a kid I always heard of some school called Gonzaga,” Wiggins said. “They always make it to March Madness, they always win, they’re always putting people in the pros, they have a good coach.”

A 13.3 point-per-game scorer last season at Florida State who made 38.7% of his 3-pointers, Wiggins is encouraged by all the possibilities at Gonzaga. The 6-10 wing has seen and enjoyed the online discourse about potential lineups featuring him next to 6-7 Davis Fogle, 6-11 Braden Huff and 7-1 Massamba Diop.

“That was really (Barsh’s) pitch and saying, with your shooting ability, we’re adding your shooting ability so that’s really going to open up things for everybody on the floor, whether that’s your shooting or B-Huff’s hook shot or Diop, with them doubling the center,” Wiggins said. “It’s just going to open up a lot. Coach Few’s system, a lot of movement, not really standing in the corner. It was a really good pitch and obviously it got me here.”

Wiggins plans to spend the next few weeks working out back home in Atlanta with a longtime personal trainer, “Coach BB” of SmallBall Training, and shooting coach Bobby Perez before moving to Spokane ahead of fall practices.

On the surface, outside shooting projects to be the most valuable asset Wiggins will bring to a Gonzaga program that posted the lowest 3-point percentage of Few’s 27-year tenure last season (34.0%). Wiggins wants to keep that aspect of his offensive game sharp, but the veteran wing is also looking to improve his ball-handling and defense.

“I’m really showing people I can be even more versatile, really just working on putting the ball on the floor more,” Wiggins said. “Rebounding more, crashing offense, defense. I’m always still working on my defense. Offense, just putting the ball on the floor, making sure the shooting is staying sharp, post game if I ever need to and touch around the basket.”

Gonzaga.title: How Chauncey Wiggins Turns Gonzaga's Frontcourt Into a Jumbo Nightmare
Gonzaga.summary: The 6-foot-10 Florida State transfer adds shooting and length to a Gonzaga basketball roster already loaded at forward, with a starting five that could run three interchangeable bigs.
Gonzaga.author: Tuck Clarry

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga star Brandon Clarke's death ruled accidental overdose of cocaine, heroin
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga forward Brandon Clarke died of an accidental overdose of heroin and cocaine, the L.A. County Medical Examiner ruled in a report released Friday.

The medical examiner also listed the “combined effects of multiple prescription medications” as a significant contributing factor in his death. A full autopsy report will be released at a later date and will include the names of those prescriptions, the medical examiner’s office said.

Clarke, a beloved teammate who spent his entire NBA career with the Memphis Grizzlies, died May 11 at a residence in Southern California. The 29-year-old former Gonzaga standout was found unresponsive in his bedroom, according to the coroner’s report.

Following his death, the Grizzlies said in a statement that they were “heartbroken by the tragic loss.” Clarke had struggled with injuries during the past three seasons, but when healthy he was one of the most impactful bench players in the NBA.

“Brandon was an outstanding teammate and an even better person whose impact on the organization and the greater Memphis community will not be forgotten,” the team wrote.

Clarke played 309 games over seven seasons for Memphis, with the team reaching the playoffs four times. The Grizzlies said Clarke was expected to make a full recovery ahead of next season. He had a year remaining on his four-year contract worth $12.5 million annually.

Clarke was pronounced dead after the Los Angeles Fire Department responded to an emergency call at a residence in the 20300 block of Del Campo Place in Woodland Hills at just after 5 p.m. May 11. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 5:15 p.m.

His death came six weeks after he was charged in Arkansas with felony counts of trafficking of a controlled substance and fleeing law enforcement at speeds topping 100 mph. Deputies alleged that he had 235 grams of kratom, a controversial plant-based substance that is not approved by the Food and Drug Administration, in a duffel bag in his car at the time of his arrest April 1.

While kratom is considered a felony narcotic in Arkansas, it was legal in Tennessee, where Clarke owned a home, at the time of his arrest. The coroner’s report did not note the presence of kratom.

Clarke was also facing misdemeanor counts of drug possession for a THC vape pen he was carrying and for making unsafe lane changes and speeding. He was scheduled to appear at an arraignment May 15 at the St. Francis County District Court in Forrest City, Arkansas. Following his death, the case was dismissed.

Clarke was born in Vancouver, Canada, and raised in Phoenix. He was part of a Gonzaga team with Los Angeles Clippers forward Rui Hachimura that was one of the greatest in school history. Clarke is remembered not only for his NCAA Division I-leading 68.7 field-goal percentage, but for his warm and kind spirit.

He was drafted in the first round of the 2019 NBA draft.

“He was just so easy to coach,” Gonzaga head coach Mark Few said. “Every time you’d see him walking around the facility, he had a smile on his face.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga makes second 5-in-5 addition with commitment from Florida State wing Chauncey Wiggins
Gonzaga.summary:
Chauncey Wiggins scored a victory in state court on Wednesday morning, securing another year of eligibility through a preliminary injunction that featured more than a dozen other players in his home state of Georgia.

By Thursday evening, the talented Florida State transfer who played two seasons at Clemson and recently appeared at NBA Summer League for the Boston Celtics had another reason to celebrate, announcing a commitment to Mark Few and Gonzaga.

Agent Daniel Hazan of Hazan Sports confirmed the wing’s commitment to On3.com’s Joe Tipton, giving Gonzaga its second “5-in-5” transfer in as many days.

Dayton point guard Javon Bennett, an All-Atlantic 10 First Team selection last season, committed to the Zags on Wednesday after being deemed eligible through a similar lawsuit in Ohio.

Dozens of players in three separate state lawsuits – Ohio, Tennessee and most recently Georgia – have taken the NCAA to court, pursuing another year of eligibility through the governing body’s new age-based eligibility rules, giving athletes five years to play five seasons.

Although the NCAA stated it wouldn’t approve a blanket waiver to include last year’s senior class, Wiggins, Bennett and others have been successful challenging the organization in state court, earning injunctions that, for the time being, should enable both to compete for Gonzaga in 2026-27.

Uncertain if another college season was in the cards, Wiggins went through the NBA draft process and joined the Celtics at Summer League in Las Vegas, where he averaged 3 points and 2 rebounds while averaging 7.7 minutes over three games.

Wiggins is able to return to college basketball because he joined the Celtics’ roster through a Summer League invite and didn’t sign an NBA two-way or Exhibit 10 contact.

While Bennett helped the Zags address one of their holes in the backcourt, Wiggins provides something different as a 6-foot-10 wing who averaged 13.3 points and 3.9 rebounds last season as a 30-game starter at Florida State.

Both players should help address outside shooting deficiencies for a program that posted the two worst 3-point percentages of Few’s tenure in successive seasons.

Bennett made 90 3’s last season at Dayton, connecting at a clip of 34.7% on seven attempts per game. Wiggins took 5.8 3’s per game at Florida State, but was one of the most efficient shooters in the ACC, making 38.7% of his attempts.

Before Florida State, Wiggins played a total of 97 games over three seasons at Clemson, appearing in 27 games as a reserve as a freshman before starting in 18 of 36 games as a sophomore and transforming into a primary starter as a junior, making 26 starts in 34 appearances. Wiggins averaged 8.3 ppg and 2.9 rpg as a junior, shooting 43.8% from the field and 36.5% as a sophomore.

The Atlanta native played on a Florida State tam that missed the postseason after finishing 18-15 overall and 10-8 in the ACC under first-year coach Luke Loucks, but he made five NCAA Tournament appearances at Clemson, getting reserve minutes in each of the Tigers’ four games during a 2024 run to the Elite Eight. Wiggins was also on Clemson’s NCAA Tournament team in 2025, scoring 10 points in an opening-round loss to McNeese State.

An experienced wing who’s played in 129 career games, Wiggins should figure into Gonzaga’s rotation and will have a chance to compete for starting minutes in the frontcourt alongside transfer center Massamba Diop (Arizona State) and returning forward Braden Huff.

Wiggins was able to move to his third school because he entered the transfer portal in the spring, months before his case was heard by a judge in state court. Upon entering, the Florida State wing was ranked by 247Sports as the 65th best overall player in the portal.

“He found the perfect style of play (at Florida State) where his size and shooting from 3 in a spaced-out and offensive system can shine,” 247Sports.com’s Travis Branham wrote earlier this week in an analysis of Wiggins. “… He isn’t a physical presence down low, but anyone in need of floor spacing will be highly interested in adding the four-star transfer.”

Wiggins’ announcement elicited a reaction on Thursday from Jalen Warley, another wing who had college stops at both Florida State and Gonzaga and spent two seasons facing the 6-foot-10 forward in the ACC.

“Great move!!” Warley wrote, commenting on an Instagram post announcing Wiggins’ commitment.

With Wiggins, the Zags have 12 players either signed or committed to the 2026-27 roster. Wiggins, Bennett and international prospects Nathan De Sousa and Izan Almansa have all committed to GU but have yet to ink financial aid agreements.

Gonzaga.title: Bremerton's Jalen Davis names Gonzaga among 10 college finalists
Gonzaga.summary:
Days after scheduling an official visit to Gonzaga, four-star combo guard Jalen Davis named Mark Few’s program as one of his 10 finalists.

The top-rated prospect from Washington in the recruiting class of 2027 will also consider Stanford, UCLA, Ole Miss, BYU, Washington, Iowa, Texas Tech, USC and TCU, he told Joe Tipton of On3.com Thursday morning.

A standout at Bremerton High, where he plays under his father Jeremiah, Davis recently told 247Sports.com’s Brandon Jenkins he’s planning to visit Gonzaga for the team’s home opener on Nov. 7 against New Mexico State.

Davis is scheduled to visit four of his other finalists – Iowa, UCLA, Stanford and Ole Miss – before closing out his fall recruiting tour with a cross-state trip to Spokane in early November.

A 6-foot-3, 165-pound combo guard known for his shot-making, Davis is rated as the top overall player in Washington and the third-best player at his position by 247Sports. The recruiting service also considers him the nation’s No. 17 overall prospect.

“Davis is a skilled guard who differentiates himself with his feel for the game, processing ability, and understanding of how to be a high-volume scorer without having to dominate the basketball,” 247Sports recruiting director Adam Finkelstein wrote of Davis. “He put up more than 23 points per game in the 3SSB season on better than 49% shooting from the floor while playing largely off the ball. He moves without the ball extremely well. He’s a good cutter, knows how to use screens, and is still a highly effective passer.

“There aren’t many players in high school basketball who can read a pindown and then make a pocket pass if the big helps on his catch, but Davis is one of them. His ability to make quick reads and decisions is one of the most impressive parts of his game.”

A Gatorade Player of the Year in Washington, Davis led Bremerton to its second straight Class 2A championship in March while averaging 31.5 points, 9.6 rebounds, 5.8 steals and 5.2 assists. He shot 63.9% from the field and 40% from the 3-point line as a junior, leading the Knights to an overall record of 26-2.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with depth, experience, Gonzaga women can focus on little things: 'Possibilities ... are vast.'
Gonzaga.summary:
Editor’s note: This is the fourth story in a multipart series examining the offseason for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program.

The Gonzaga women’s basketball team is two months away from measuring how much offseason individual improvement has taken place.

GU coach Lisa Fortier anticipates a much more cohesive and versatile team than a year ago.

“We have the pieces in each position group that we put out there,” Fortier said. “We just have to figure out how we take them to the next level, how do we take our team shooting to the next level, how do we take our team rebounding to the next level and how do we learn to guard better as a group.”

Going into the 2025-26 season, the Zags had many unanswered questions. It started with experience – mostly experience in a Gonzaga uniform. The Bulldogs returned one starter.

There should be a marked difference in 2026-27. The Zags return four starters and five others who saw consistent time off the bench. The nine players will account for most of the playing time with two transfers and a freshman as the lone newcomers.

“We’re not freshmen to college, we’re not freshmen to workouts, we’re not freshmen to practice and pressure and those things,” Fortier said.

Gonzaga is coming off a 24-10 season that ended with an 81-66 loss to Ole Miss in an NCAA Tournament opener. The Zags hope to use how they finished in that game as a springboard into bigger and better things this year.

“We should have some confidence that we’re a good team,” Fortier said. “There are a lot of people who made big impacts that are back. I would hope that they want to keep chasing improvement, knowing what the possibilities are for this team. There’s a lot of possibilities for what this team can do.”

It’s not getting too far ahead to talk about where Fortier wants to see this team specifically and the program in general go.

“We can be a pretty good team … the possibilities for this team are vast,” she said. “Things we’ve never done before are attainable with this group. We’re just working to stay true to the process. We’ve got to work on how we show up for every individual workout and how we show up for every weight (conditioning) session. The little things done well will add up to big things.”

The Zags finished as the No. 1-ranked team in the nation in 3-point made percentage (39.2), just ahead of UConn.

Gonzaga should increase that percentage this season with capable long-distance threats. Junior-to-be guard Allie Turner led at 47.1% (89 of 189), followed by junior guard Teryn Gardner (46%, 52 of 113). Sophomore forward Lauren Whittaker made 35.5% (33 of 93) but wants to make significant improvement this season. Others are expected to shoot effectively from long range as well.

The Zags’ versatile offense will assist in shooting percentages, to be sure. When defenses are forced to account for the 6-foot-3 Whittaker, 6-2 sophomore forward Jaiden Haile and 6-2 senior forward Taylor Smith will give perimeter players plenty of open looks.

Another forward, 6-foot graduate transfer Sierra Lichtie, who was slowed by injuries last year, had a season of eligibility left but decided to move on after finishing work on a master’s degree, Fortier said.

Gonzaga outrebounded opponents by 10 per game last year. That, too, is an area Fortier expects improvement.

The Zags also will emphasize upgrades defensively. They allowed opponents 65 points per game last year, and opponents shot 40% from the field.

Position-by-position defense will be key, but Fortier said the Zags are better when they defend as a team. Better defense means the offense can play freely and doesn’t have to outscore opponents to cover for defensive liabilities.

“We need to embrace some team defensive things,” Fortier said. “How do we learn how to guard as a group, guard better individually but also find a way to help each other and cover for each other a little more? That’s an area we struggled with at different times last year.”

By and large, though, the Zags have few questions to answer going into the season. The roles of the two transfers and lone incoming freshman will be among first order of business when preseason practice begins.

The 2026-27 roster includes the fewest first-year Zags since 2023-24, when Gonzaga added two freshmen and no transfers.

Gonzaga had to use the transfer portal the last two years to replenish a roster hit by graduation and transfers. The Zags brought in four transfers two years ago and four more last season.

Turner was the lone freshman added two years ago and Haile, Julia Wilson and now-departed Paige Lofing made up last season’s freshman class.

The newest additions this season are 6-1 freshman forward Abby Lusk of Pocatello, Idaho; 6-foot junior wing/small forward Emmy Roach, a transfer from Rider; and 5-6 senior guard Jocelyn Medina, a transfer from Denver.

With a deep returning roster, it’s unlikely any of the newcomers will challenge for a starting position. But they will definitely be in the mix for valuable minutes off the bench.

Of the three newbies, Lusk may have an opportunity to make the biggest impact. Out of necessity, she had to play point guard for her high school team last year, leading Pocatello to a state championship.

“She’s perfect for us,” Fortier said. “She’s versatile. She plays with great pace. She wants to get better. She can handle the basketball. She has all the tools. It’s always an adjustment to go from high school to college, but if you don’t have the tools in high school then it’s even harder to build them in college. She’s starting off with the appropriate skill set. We did not miss on the type of kid we got with Abby.”

Gonzaga.title: Dayton's Javon Bennett commits to Gonzaga after securing extra year through Ohio ruling
Gonzaga.summary:
A recent court ruling in Ohio has enabled Gonzaga to fill one of its vacant backcourt spots three months before the start of the college basketball season.

Javon Bennett, a 5-foot-10 point guard who earned All-Atlantic 10 first-team honors last season at Dayton, committed to the Zags on Wednesday after securing a fifth season of eligibility three weeks ago through a preliminary injunction in Ohio.

Bennett’s agent, Harrison Gaines, confirmed the player’s commitment to Joe Tipton of On3.com.

A veteran guard who appeared in 136 college basketball games over four seasons at Merrimack and Dayton, Bennett was one of the 15 student-athletes who filed a lawsuit against the NCAA in Ohio, claiming they should be eligible to return for a fifth season through the governing body’s new age-based eligibility model, also known as the “5-for-5” rule.

With only eight players signed to financial aid agreements as of Wednesday, Gonzaga is in a position to add multiple players in the coming weeks, and desperately needed to address its depth in the backcourt after combo guard Jack Kayil kept his name in the NBA draft and starting point guard Mario Saint-Supery signed a professional contract with Valencia in early July.

Pending other roster moves, Bennett could be a candidate to start at point guard after averaging 15.8 points, 2.9 assists and 2.2 rebounds last season for a Dayton team that advanced to the quarterfinals of the National Invitational Tournament (NIT). Bennett’s 3-point shooting numbers have been up and down the last four years, but he made 34.7% of his shots from behind the arc last season while attempting a career-high seven 3s per game.

As of Wednesday, the Zags had just one other backcourt player with prior D-I experience signed to the 2026-27 roster – Houston transfer Isiah Harwell – but nobody with experience as a primary ball-handler. Gonzaga picked up a commitment from 23-year-old Cholet point guard Nathan De Sousa in June, but the Frenchman is still awaiting NCAA clearance and hasn’t formally been announced by the school.

A native of Orlando, Bennett played his freshman season at Merrimack, where he was named the Northeast Conference Rookie of the Year in 2022-23 while helping the Warriors capture regular season and conference tournament championships. As a school recently transitioning from the Division II level, Merrimack was unable to participate in the NCAA Tournament and its bid automatically went to Northeast Conference runner-up Fairleigh Dickinson, which went on to upset top-seeded Purdue in the opening round.

After averaging 9.6 ppg, 3.4 apg and 2.9 spg as a freshman, Bennett transferred to Dayton and started in 28 of 31 games for a Flyers team that won an NCAA Tournament opener against Nevada before losing to former GU assistant Tommy Lloyd and Arizona in the Round of 32. The point guard averaged 8.4 ppg, 3.3 apg and 2.1 rpg while shooting 39.3% from the field and 31.6% from the 3-point line.

Bennett averaged double figures for the first time in his career as a junior, scoring 11.6 ppg to go with 2.7 rpg and 2.1 apg, starting in 33 of 34 games for Dayton. He shot a career-best 39% from the 3-point line while shooting better than 40% from the field (43.7%) for the first time in his career.

As a senior, Bennett posted career-best scoring numbers and nearly led the Flyers to another NCAA Tournament berth, ultimately losing in the Atlantic 10 championship to VCU. Bennett had at least 20 points in 11 games last season, recording a season-high 27 against Saint Bonaventure in the A-10 Tournament quarterfinals. His career high of 30 points came the year prior during an NIT opener against Florida Atlantic.

Bennett becomes Gonzaga’s third addition via the transfer portal this offseason, joining Houston’s Harwell and Arizona State center Massamba Diop, both of whom signed with Mark Few’s program in May.

Gonzaga’s ability to add to its transfer class and fill remaining scholarship spots could hinge on eligibility rulings in various states. Since the Ohio injunction cleared the way for Bennett and others to secure another year of eligibility, athletes in three other states have prevailed in similar lawsuits.

The Athletic listed Bennett in the Honorable Mention portion of a list detailing the top 10 players who could return to college basketball in 2026-27. Another ranking compiled by On3.com listed Bennett at No. 5.

Oregon State.title: The 2026 College Football Season Begins
Oregon State.summary:
The Oregon State football program will begin their 2026-2027 campaign on Saturday morning with a road game against the Houston Cougars. After a very long offseason in which JaMarcus Shephard was introduced as the program's latest head coach, what should the expectations be for the Beavers' new season? 

Your host Matt Bagley gives his thoughts on Oregon State's potential in the first year of the rebuild. Bagley also makes some predictions for the greater Pac-12 season ahead and who we could see contend for the college football championship at the end of the year. Plus, the return of five games to watch in the Week One slate.

You'll also hear audio from Shephard's media availability ahead of the Houston game, as the clock ticks toward kickoff. Go Beavs.

Washington State.title: Getting to know WSU's next opponent, Kansas State | Q&A with beat writer Ryan Gilbert
Washington State.summary:
To preview Washington State’s next game, a road test against Big 12 foe Kansas State, The Spokesman-Review conferred with K-State beat writer Ryan Gilbert, who covers the Wildcats for GoPowercat.

Here is our Q&A.

1. How did K-State’s offensive line look against Nicholls, and do the injuries to John Pastore and George Fitzpatrick look to hamper the Cats as much as it might seem?

The offensive line checked all the boxes it could on Saturday. There were a lot of questions surrounding this group entering the season, but game No. 1 was a success. That being said, Nicholls is just not a good football team, so it’s tough to get too excited over that performance in the trenches. K-State simply had the bigger, more physically dominant dudes at the point of contact. Anything other than a promising night would have been a concern for the offensive line.

George Fitzpatrick not being able to give it a go didn’t help matters, but Collin Klein & Co. certainly couldn’t have been caught off guard when they learned he had to be sidelined this season. His health condition from last offseason just lingered and lingered, so it’s not like this just happened out of nowhere. There was ample time to create a backup plan. John Pastore, though, was supposed to be not just a starter but a true star at left tackle. His injury, which will sideline him for the season, happened about a month before the season, and then Tanner Morley also had to miss some time late in camp, so everything kind of just compounded at once.

But the short answer here is that Pastore’s injury is a big blow to the offensive line. Not having him in 2026 will sting. And there have been a lot of moving pieces in the last 30 days due to all the injuries. Offensive lines have to jell together, and, well, it’s hard to jell in just a matter of days.

If there’s one thing I took away from Washington State after catching parts of Sunday’s game against Washington, it’s that the Cougars defensive front can really give their team a chance to win this game. If K-State has just an average offensive line this game (or this season), that’d be a success given the circumstances.

2. Who are the main playmakers in K-State’s defense?

Ahead of the season, the easy answer would have been Oklahoma State transfer Wendell Gregory. But against Nicholls, the junior defensive end really didn’t do much. Of course, it’s way too early to write him off, but many expected him to absolutely feast in 2026, and to not move the needle against an FCS program isn’t exactly promising.

While Gregory had a quiet game, Darien Whitaker stepped up with a strip sack. It seems like his stock is really rising. While he’s listed as a linebacker, expect to see him line up at the edge on defense.

A couple of guys had great games against Nicholls, though – linebacker Gabe Powers and safety Logan Bartley. Powers, who previously spent time at Ohio State, was listed as a starter on the depth chart ahead of the first game, but nobody expected him to have the impact he did. He was great. Meanwhile, Bartley was much the same story – just a solid piece who had some big hits in the secondary.

It’s also worth noting that linebacker Mekhi Mason’s status for Saturday is up in the air due to injury. He’ll be worth monitoring as the teams go through warmups, as he’s a prominent piece on defense.

3. How could Cougar fans expect the Cats to use their tight ends, which has been a strength of the program for quite a while?

As a former five-star, there shouldn’t need to be any endorsement given to tight end Linkon Cure. His upside is clearly there. However, we just haven’t seen him impact the game in a purple jersey. His freshman year in 2025 was very underwhelming, and Saturday against Nicholls was bland. The only direction for him to go is up, but he’s got plenty of meat left on the bone. He’s a player to definitely keep a sharp eye on, but to say he’s a true difference-maker right now would be a bit rich.

Fellow tight end Garrett Oakley has been in the program for as long as QB Avery Johnson has, so these two obviously have a great connection. Many deem him to be one of the top tight ends in the Big 12. Last season, Oakley dropped countless routine passes, so as long as he can simply hang on to the football, Oakley is definitely a red zone threat for the offense.

4. How much can you take away from such a lopsided win over an FCS team?

There are certain areas worth investing more into than others. For example, as we talked about, the offensive line looked good simply because of how bad Nicholls was.

On the flip side, though, K-State’s effort, focus, execution and buy-in were at a top-notch level. The Cats committed only one penalty on Saturday – that has nothing to do with Nicholls.

Overall, take it all with a grain of salt, but you can’t fault a group for simply beating the team that lied on its schedule.

5. What are the main strengths of RBs Rodney Fields and Joe Jackson, and is there any way WSU could slow them down?

It was pretty surprising to see Rodney Fields get the start at the running back spot, as pretty much everyone assumed Joe Jackson would technically be RB1. But that speaks more to how good Fields was in camp than anything. Fields and Jackson are very quality backs.

Just take a look at what Jackson did against Utah last season. He can absolutely be your workhorse.

Fields, on the other hand, has great speed and vision.

Lastly, Jay Harris is definitely in the doghouse after a fumble against Nicholls, so we’ll see how much he plays, but he certainly is worth mentioning. He is, in fact, the clear RB3, but he’s a lot closer to being the third head of a three-headed monster than he is to riding the bench for the entire game.

Washington State.title: WSU faces tough test on the road, UW should cruise at home | Picks of the week
Washington State.summary:
Arizona State coach Kenny Dillingham has proven himself an expert in developing quarterbacks during his three seasons in Tempe. His program also has performed exceedingly well as a road underdog. Those matters are linked, of course, and the latest test of their interconnectivity comes Saturday.

The Sun Devils are 14.5-point underdogs at Texas A&M. How quarterback Cutter Boley performs will determine whether they are within striking range of the 10th-ranked Aggies in the fourth quarter — and, by extension, whether the Big 12 is positioned to collect what would be a first-class victory.

To this point, Dillingham has excelled in comparable situations: He’s 4-1 against the spread as a double-digit underdog away from home since taking charge of his alma mater.

The Sun Devils covered the spread as double-digit underdogs at Cal, Washington and UCLA in 2023 – they beat the Bruins straight up, in fact – and against Texas in the epic 2024 College Football Playoff quarterfinal. The lone failure to cover was at Utah three years ago.

Boley has started one game for the Sun Devils, the 70-7 home victory over Morgan State last weekend that will have zero relevance Saturday morning. In College Station, he will face a talented, well-coached defense and the din generated by 102,000 fans.

But Boley has experience with SEC crowds from his two-year tenure at Kentucky. The key numbers aren’t stellar: He threw five touchdowns and nine interceptions in road games against South Carolina, Georgia, Auburn, Vanderbilt, Florida and Texas.

Which brings us to the Dillingham-as-QB-whisperer component.

Can he conjure a crisp, efficient performance from Boley that looks nothing like the junior’s previous showings in SEC stadiums?

If so, the Sun Devils will be positioned to record a major upset that would both elevate their profile and do wonders for the Big 12, which desperately needs a breakthrough victory in one of several Week 2 matchups against SEC and Big Ten opponents.

Non-conference success, especially against the two leagues that dominate the sport, could lead to the Big 12 placing an at-large team in the College Football Playoff.

Someone needs to step forward. Given Dillingham’s knack for upside surprises, Arizona State is an option worth monitoring.

To the Week 2 picks …

(All times Pacific)

Washington State (+18.5) at Kansas State

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on TNT

Comment: The logistics are daunting for WSU, which played a taxing game Sunday in Seattle and is traveling halfway across the country — on a short week, no less — to play an early (body clock) game in the heat against a host that cruised to victory last weekend. Pick: Kansas State

Oregon (-18.5) at Oklahoma State

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Ducks didn’t look like a team that can win the national championship in their narrow victory over Boise State, but the Cowboys didn’t look like a team that can win any games in their loss to Tulsa. We’ve seen this script from the Ducks before. Dan Lanning will have them ready to roll. Pick: Oregon

Oklahoma (+2.5) at Michigan

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on Fox

Comment: It was bad enough that Michigan needed a controversial extra second to beat Western Michigan. But quarterback Bryce Underwood isn’t responding well to the criticism, including a warning from coach Kyle Whittingham that his play must improve. Meanwhile, the Sooners are loaded on defense. Pick: Oklahoma

Arizona State (+14.5) at Texas A&M

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ABC

Comment: The Texas heat won’t be a problem for the Sun Devils, but the Kyle Field crowd could cause communication problems early. We expect a slow start and strong finish from the visitors. And for the game to be in doubt with five minutes remaining. Pick: Arizona State

Utah State (+26.5) at Washington

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: If the Huskies play the way they did in the Apple Cup, they will win by 20. If they play better than they did in the Apple Cup, they will win by 40. Or didn’t you notice that Utah State lost at home to Idaho State by double digits? Yikes. Pick: Washington

Arizona (+7.5) at BYU

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Fox

Comment: This has the potential to be one of the best games of the day, anywhere. After all, the teams went to double overtime in Tucson 11 months ago, and the competitive balance hasn’t changed significantly. The Cougars pose a supreme test of Arizona’s defensive front, which couldn’t stop BYU’s ground game (258 yards) last year. The winner jumps to the head of the line in the Big 12 title race. Pick: BYU

Cal (+3.5) at Syracuse

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on ACC Network

Comment: A demoralizing loss in the opener, followed by a long trip to face a low-profile opponent that generates zero urgency? Feels like a trap game for the Bears, even though winless teams with new coaches should not be in position to get trapped. Pick: Syracuse

Memphis (+8.5) at Boise State

Kickoff: 3 p.m. on USA Network

Comment: No game in Week 2 carries greater playoff implications, not even the Texas-Ohio State showdown. After all, there is only one playoff berth reserved for the best team in the Group of Five, and the winner in Boise instantly becomes the favorite. The Broncos looked like a CFP team last weekend at Oregon. They need a comparable performance Saturday. Pick: Memphis

San Diego State (+12.5) at UCLA

Kickoff: 4:15 p.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: The Bruins are soaring with confidence after opening the Bob Chesney era with a convincing victory at Cal. Do the Aztecs have enough on the lines of scrimmage to stand tall for 60 minutes? Is SDSU quarterback Jayden Denegal capable of an error-free game against a Big Ten defense? We aren’t convinced on either front. Pick: UCLA

Ohio State (+1.5) at Texas

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on ABC

Comment: The best non-conference duel of the season is a rematch of Ohio State’s 14-7 victory last year. That was the season opener for both teams, and Texas quarterback Arch Manning looked rattled throughout. He should be sharper this time against a reloading Buckeyes defense. Enjoy it, folks. If the playoff expands to 24 teams next year, these blue-blood showdowns will have far lower stakes. Pick: Texas

Texas Tech (+26.5) at Oregon State

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on CBS

Comment: The Beavers were grittier than expected in their opener under new coach JaMarcus Shepard, a 13-point loss at Houston. Meanwhile, Texas Tech was slightly less than overwhelming against Abilene Christian. If OSU quarterback Braden Atkinson avoids major mistakes, the Red Raiders could have trouble clearing the high bar set by the oddsmakers. Pick: Oregon State

Arkansas (+12.5) at Utah

Kickoff: 7:15 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: One of the few Big 12 vs. SEC matchups this season should not be competitive in the fourth quarter: The Utes have too many playmakers for Arkansas, which is rebuilding under coach Ryan Silverfield and lacks the high-end talent present on so many SEC rosters. If the Utes win, they should be undefeated entering the back half of the schedule in late October. Pick: Utah

Straight-up winners: Oregon, Oklahoma, Texas A&M, Kansas State, Washington, BYU, Syracuse, Boise State, UCLA, Texas, Texas Tech and Utah

Washington State.title: 'I started sobbing': Behind WSU LB Keith Brown's return to action after missing last season to injury
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The moment began to wash over Keith Brown some 10 minutes before kickoff, the gravity hitting him like a tsunami. He sat in his locker inside Husky Stadium, waiting to take the field for Sunday’s Apple Cup, the nervous energy of tens of thousands of fans pounding outside the steel walls. He had waited six years for his moment, a chance to start a season opener, an opportunity to demonstrate his arrival at Washington State.

For a moment, the senior linebacker looked up and glanced to his left, where he saw veteran wide receiver Darrius Clemons with a bit of moisture around his eyes.

That’s when it hit Brown.

“I started sobbing,” Brown said.

Right before the biggest moment of his college career, the first game of his sixth and final season, Brown felt everything crash over him at once: the two years at Oregon, the redshirt year at Louisville, the first year at WSU and then the second, which he missed due to a shoulder injury. He had started a handful of games as a freshman five years ago, but never a season opener, a signal that he had never been the guy.

Now he is. He’s one of WSU’s two starting linebackers. On Sunday, he was entrusted with some of the game’s biggest moments, like the Cougars’ goal-line stop right before halftime. He led the team with six tackles, all solo, illustrating the level of playmaking that made him the top-rated prospect in all of Oregon during high school.

“Missing last year was really hard for me,” Brown said. “And then, I’ve waited my turn six years to start Week 1, so yeah, it was a really emotional moment for me. It felt good to be out there again, it really did.”

Brown certainly played like it. Right before halftime, the Huskies had fourth-and-goal from the Cougars’ 1-yard line, threatening to go up three scores. Things were tilting for WSU, whose offense was slogging and scuffling through a slow start to the game. Go down three scores here and the visitors’ path to a comeback would become just about impossible.

So Brown leapt into action. UW quarterback Demond Williams Jr. took a shotgun snap and handed it off to running back Jayden Limar, who plunged up the middle. He was met in the gap by a host of Cougar defenders. In the middle was Brown, who wrapped Limar up around the midsection and drove him backward. A sea of WSU defenders surged into the pile, forcing officials to blow the play dead before Limar could generate any more forward momentum.

Thinking back on the play now, Brown remembers his assignment: He was to look at center Kolt Dietrich and make his move accordingly. If Dietrich went left, Brown would pursue off his right hip, and vice versa. He figured he would have to wade through a mass of bodies if he wanted to make the stop.

“And when I was running through the gap, a guy showed up in front of me,” Brown laughed. “I didn’t realize it was Jirah who threw him around.”

Turns out, Brown realized after the fact, that WSU defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepetele hadn’t just won his rep against UW left guard John Mills, a consensus freshman All-American last season. He had thrown him to the left, paving the way for Brown to meet Limar in the gap. Several Cougar defenders converged to create a pile-up and push Limar back, but the stop began with Leaupepetele and his physicality up front.

“Kudos to Jirah for being as grown as he is,” Brown said.

Across the next 90 minutes or so, Brown and the Cougars’ defense continued to make things hard on the Huskies, who needed two fourth-quarter touchdowns – and one critical third-down conversion with about two minutes to play – to finally put away Kirby Moore’s team for good. But all things considered, Brown says he feels good about what he and his unit put on display in Seattle, giving their team a chance to draw within one in the fourth quarter on two different occasions.

This week, as Washington State prepares for a road test against Big 12 foe Kansas State, Brown says the emotions he felt before Sunday’s game haven’t followed him around. He’s trying to stay in the moment, he says, keeping blinders on ahead of another critical Power Four game. As one of the leaders of this defense, Brown finds it important to stay even-keeled and focused.

Part of that, he says, has required changing his approach to the season. Toward the end of the Cougars’ fall camp, Brown and the WSU defense had been flourishing, becoming the story of camp. “We were feeling on top of the world,” Brown said. Then one day, that unit turned in a forgettable practice, and defensive coordinator Trent Bray let them hear about it. He encouraged his players to delete all social media apps off their phones, including Instagram and Twitter, so that they wouldn’t see posts about themselves and get too high or low.

As he thought about it, Brown realized he agreed. He would rather not see articles about him and his team, positive or negative. Sometimes they still find their way to his phone thanks to his mom, Sarah – “I’m like, ‘Mom, I don’t want to see them,’ ” Brown said with a smile – but the decision is still helping Brown block out the outside noise.

“I could easily think that I’m this or I’m that,” Brown said. “But realistically, I have to get better every week. If you even look back on it, I still didn’t play my best game, not even close. I left some on the table. There’s reads I could have filled faster and stuff like that, but yeah, every week just wanna get better.”

“Keith is as consistent as it gets,” WSU defensive end Linus Zunk said. “I mean, I’ve been able to practice alongside him for a long time now, so really out there, it’s just replicating what I already see of him in practice and the way that he communicates and keeps the defense together. So he’s definitely doing a great job in that.”

Mostly, though, Brown just appreciates the opportunity to do so in the first place.

***

A little more than a year later, Brown calls it a “stupid mistake by the two of us.” It was early in fall camp last season, and on a sweltering afternoon at Rogers Practice Field, he got into it with running back Kirby Vorhees. The two argued and things turned physical. In the heat of the moment, Brown got his shoulder tangled up with Vorhees before they were separated by their teammates.

At first, Brown remembers, he didn’t think the injury was serious. Moments after the scuffle, he worked with trainer Brian Oelke to pop his shoulder back into place.

“I was like, all right, doesn’t feel too bad,” Brown said. “I was gonna continue practicing.”

But Oelke advised against it, holding Brown out of the rest of the practice. The next morning, Brown woke and realized things could be serious. “I couldn’t even sit up,” he said. “It was more serious than I thought it was at all.”

So Brown had his shoulder checked out. He went through examinations, an X-ray and an MRI, which showed a labrum tear, which Brown could have played through. Doctors expected that much. What they weren’t prepared for were the results of an MRI, which showed additional bone breakage around the tear, which made the injury serious, risking the stability of the entire shoulder.

So Brown consulted with team medical director and orthopaedic surgeon Ed Tingstad, who told Brown, “You’re an adult. At the end of the day, you can make your own decision.” Brown chatted with former coaches, former teammates. “Everyone was kinda pointing in the direction of, if I were to play last year, I would have to get surgery after the year no matter what, and then I’d miss all of training, pro day and stuff like that. So I was like, OK, let’s just get surgery and try it again.”

Brown admits that at first, he had a hard time accepting that his season would end before it even started, that he wouldn’t get a chance to play in the middle of what turned out to be one of the country’s best defenses. That fall, the Cougars went on to give legitimate scares to Power Four opponents like Ole Miss and Virginia, both one-score contests in the fourth quarter.

Brown always tuned into those. That year, he was teammates with former running back Dylan Paine, who was also out with an injury. They set up a system: During games, they would be in their rooms on a Discord call with each other. On one screen, they had a monitor to play a video game called Arc Raiders. On the other, they would have the broadcast of the WSU game, chatting with each other about the video game and the football game.

Around that time, Brown says, he had gotten over the initial shock of missing the season – “I was like, OK, it is what it is, let’s attack this,” he said of his surgery – but the thought of being able to make an impact in those games, in the Cougars’ close defeats to the likes of Ole Miss and Virginia and James Madison, pulled at him.

“Those are games you want to play in,” he said. “I love playing big games. It’s always something I’ve really enjoyed. It is hard to watch. It is for sure. You always root for your teammates, obviously, but you’re like, dang, I wish I was out there, you know?”

By the spring, he was. He was cleared to return to action ahead of WSU’s spring ball. At first, he says, he felt a bit anxious about putting his shoulder to the test. But he trusted the advice of Tingstad, who reassured Brown that, yes, his shoulder might sting a bit the first few times he made contact with a teammate or a sled. But unless something drastic happens, Tingstad told Brown, he wouldn’t reinjure it. Even better for Brown: He didn’t have any scar tissue, which some athletes get after surgery.

Then came summertime, when Brown felt even more like himself. He became roommates with Vorhees, who he considers one of his closer friends on the team. At around 7 a.m. on Saturday mornings, Brown says, he would often hear Vorhees banging on his desk in frustration. He was playing Fortnite, Brown realized later on.

It’s a moment Brown laughs about in hindsight, like others recently. Neither Brown nor Vorhees took their tussle personally. It was just two competitors letting their tempers flare for a moment, Brown says now, chalking it up to a hot day and a deep sense of wanting to win.

As his final season of college football unfolds, Brown feels that more than ever. He wants to make this season count, wants to squeeze every last drop out of this experience. It’s why he deleted all social media off his phone. It’s why he practices hard and watches game film even harder.

Has the finality of it all hit Brown, who has been playing college football since 2021? Not yet, he says. He’s more focused on taking things week-by-week, and this week, that means honing on K-State and the Wildcats’ offense. Last weekend, he felt the emotions hit him like a Mack truck. Not since.

“It’ll probably hit me again on senior night when my mom and everyone’s out there and stuff like that. It’ll probably hit me again after the bowl game,” Brown said. “I think throughout the weeks and stuff like that, you don’t really think about it. You just prepare and go play.”

Washington State.title: Cougars Fall to Washington in Apple Cup, 24-10
In Apple Cup loss to Washington, Cougars' third-down woes might have more to do with first and second down | WSU rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Have your pick at what could be the biggest problem Washington State faced on offense in Sunday’s Apple Cup loss to Washington.

Could it be the Cougars’ turnover problem? Sure, they lost three. What about their running game? Possibly. They got only 48 combined yards from their running backs . How about their inefficiency in the kicking game? That’s valid too . Kicker Jack Stevens misfired on two field goals, including one that was moved back five yards following a pre-snap penalty.

The one that looms perhaps the largest, though, is that WSU went 0-for-11 on third down. Good luck winning many games with that. In fact, it bothered quarterback Caden Pinnick so much that in a postgame news conference, he cut himself off from an answer on a different topic to say this: “I’m just thinking about the 0-for-11 right now.”

That made things nearly impossible for the Cougars’ offense, even when they climbed back into the game with two scores in the fourth quarter: a rushing touchdown from Pinnick and a field goal from Stevens, both of which pulled the Cougs to within one score.

But here’s the interesting rub about that number: Rough as WSU’s day on third down was, the Cougars put themselves in some tough situations thanks to their first- and second-down plays. That set up several challenging third -down looks, including two third-and-longs and three third-and-shorts. WSU’s average yards-to-go on third down was about 7, which is far from an easy situation, especially in a raucous Husky Stadium.

After the game, WSU coach Kirby Moore seemed to be aware of the problem, possibly without seeing the numbers first: “You gotta go back to first and second down first, and we gotta be more efficient,” Moore said. “We gotta create more explosives there on first and second down. And then third -and -long and XL, they’ve got a really good front, and sometimes that front was getting there a little bit quicker than we wanted it to. So that’s something we gotta look at.”

Here are a few numbers that illustrate the point.

On first down, the Cougars mostly excelled, averaging 7 yards per play. They ran 12 rushes for a total of 70 yards, which is an average rush of 5.8 yards. Pinnick also completed 10 of 12 passes on first down for 107 yards, an average of 10.7 yards per play.

But the Cougars also got behind the chains on a couple occasions. In one scenario, left guard Kyle Martin was called for a false start, underscoring his forgettable first start at the college level. And on another first down, WSU lost 2 yards, resulting in a second-and-12. That’s no way to take down a Husky defense that’s already on track to live up to its billing as one of the country’s best units this fall.

For WSU, the bigger problem came on second down. The Cougars rushed seven times for a total of 17 yards, an average of 2.4 yards. That’s about a 1.5-yard difference from their output on first down, largely explained by their insistence on running up the middle, which often went nowhere. That’s one adjustment WSU offensive coordinator Matt Miller would be wise to make headed into Saturday’s game at Kansas State.

Here are Pinnick’s numbers on second down: 5-for-10 passing for 30 yards and one interception, which came on a dropped pass in the fourth quarter. Pinnick also took one sack on second down, which resulted in a 4-yard loss.

Overall, WSU’s second-down plays went for an average of 2.4 yards.

“We gotta be more efficient and explosive on first and second down, and create more manageable third downs,” Moore said. “Third-and-7-plus against anyone in college football, it’s gonna be difficult. The protection’s gotta hold up. Obviously, routes downfield. The defense usually has an advantage in those situations, so we have to do a better job on first and second down.”

It’s no secret that the Cougs slogged through a bleak third-down effort, and while they could have remedied that problem with better efficiency on first and second down, third downs are a part of the game. For the game, they averaged a shade under 2 yards per play on third down.

They also took two sacks on third down. WSU’s offensive line gave up 13 quarterback pressures, according to Pro Football Focus, four apiece from Martin and right tackle Jonny Lester, plus three from right guard Nick Bakken and two from center Noah Dunham. The Cougars likely won’t play a better defense than the Huskies’ this season, but those numbers must improve for their offense to follow suit.

At the same time, though, the bigger problem in the Cougars’ third-down scenarios actually seems to be the first- and second-down scenarios that precede them. Look for Moore and Miller to make adjustments accordingly before they embark on their second straight Power 4 tilt to open the season.

Washington State.title: WSU heads to the Midwest to take on Kansas State in second-straight Power 4 game to open season | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s road game against Kansas State on Saturday morning.

What is it? In the teams’ first meeting, Washington State heads to the Midwest to take on Big 12 foe Kansas State, which is coming off a lopsided 71-3 win over FCS Nicholls. The home-and-home series, which includes a 2029 matchup in Pullman, was brokered in 2016 by former WSU president Kirk Schulz – who had recently held the same position at K-State.

It’s the second straight road Power 4 game to open the season for the Cougars, who are coming off a loss in Sunday’s Apple Cup to No. 17 Washington.

Where is it? Bill Snyder Family Stadium in Manhattan, Kansas.

When is it? Kickoff is set for 9 a.m. (11 a.m. local time)

Where can I watch it? TNT will broadcast the game, with streaming available on HBO Max.

Who is favored? As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around an 181/2-point underdog in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week? In a 24-10 loss to No. 17 Washington in the first season-opening Apple Cup, WSU’s offense struggled to the tune of three turnovers, two missed field goals and a third-down conversion rate of 0-for-11. The Cougars made things interesting in the fourth quarter – quarterback Caden Pinnick scored on an 11-yard rushing touchdown and kicker Jack Stevens connected on a field goal – but their defense, staunch for the majority of the game, couldn’t produce stops on the ensuing drives.

In WSU coach Kirby Moore’s debut game, the Cougs’ defense shone the most, holding the No. 17 Huskies and quarterback Demond Williams Jr. to just 10 points through three quarters. That included a key goal-line stop right before halftime, when WSU linebacker Keith Brown led the charge in stuffing UW running back Jayden Limar on fourth-and-goal from the 1, sending the visitors into the locker room with a boatload of momentum.

But as was the case for the majority of the game, WSU’s offense couldn’t cash in. In his debut as the Cougars’ new quarterback, the UC Davis transfer Pinnick completed 16 of 25 passes for 142 yards and two interceptions, one of which came on a dropped pass in the fourth quarter. He also registered one rushing touchdown, an 11-yard designed keeper in the fourth quarter, pulling WSU to within 10-7.

“We gotta make sure – and this is overall from an offensive standpoint – our first goal was 100% ball security,” Moore said on Monday. “We did not achieve that, so we gotta do a better job taking care of the football. Had an initial really good start on the first drive. Got in some longer down and distances there on the third downs, which are difficult, and sometimes the defense has a say in the fight, and you gotta be ready to check the ball down, take care of the football. Sometimes it’s OK to punt, and that’s something we gotta really emphasize. Great job responding there in the fourth quarter, and so we gotta build on that.”

In a critical development, the Cougars also lost veteran receiver/kick returner Tony Freeman to an injury. After just 10 snaps, Freeman went down in the first quarter, went to the locker room and returned in street clothes, out for the rest of the game. On Monday, Moore indicated Freeman is likely to miss Saturday’s game with a knee injury, adding that coaches are still waiting on the results of Freeman’s MRI.

On offense, WSU also got impressive games from receivers Daniel Blood (five catches for 57 yards) and Darrius Clemons (three catches for 40 yards). If Freeman misses Saturday’s game, those two will have to step up again for the Cougars, who could also ask more from receivers Tank Hawkins and Branden Ganashamoorthy.

The Cougars’ defense was led by the veteran linebacker Brown, who missed all of last season recovering from a shoulder injury he sustained during fall camp. In Sunday’s game, he looked like he never missed a beat, leading the team with six tackles, all solo.

Scouting Kansas State … K-State opened the season last weekend with a 71-3 romp over FCS Nicholls, which was no match for the Wildcats, who are led by senior quarterback Avery Johnson. In his first game of his final season of college football, he completed 15 of 21 passes for 199 yards and three touchdowns, exiting midway through the third quarter as the Wildcats continued to roll.

K-State has two top running backs: Oklahoma State transfer Rodney Fields, who made a surprise start in Saturday’s game and churned out 14 carries for 101 yards and one score; and veteran returner Joe Jackson, who added seven rushes for 38 yards and one touchdown. All told, seven Wildcats scored touchdowns: Johnson, Fields, Jackson (two), receivers Jaron Tibbs Josh Manning and Brandon White (punt return), plus reserves Jacob Knuth and Monterrio Elston Jr.

It’s the debut season for head coach Collin Klein, who starred as K-State’s quarterback in the early 2010s and went on to become an assistant coach with the Wildcats from 2017-23, then worked as Texas A&M’s offensive coordinator for the 2024 and 2025 seasons before returning to his alma mater as the head coach for this season.

Some names to watch on K-State’s defense include linebacker Gabe Powers and safety Logan Bartley, who tied for a team-leading five tackles against Nicholls, plus Oklahoma State transfer edge rusher Wendell Gregory, who is expected to be one of the Big 12’s best edge rushers this season. In Saturday’s game, the Wildcats piled up 10 tackles for loss, including 1.5 from defensive end Jordan Allen.

“Lot of different sets offensively,” Moore said of Kansas State’s offense. “They do a great job of running the football. The quarterback’s part of it. A lot of different schemes, and then when you get tight, they have a lot of play action concepts that get guys vertically down the field.”

What happened last time?

This is the teams’ first meeting.
