Washington State.title: LB Keith Brown leads the way in WSU defense's sterling showing in Apple Cup loss to No. 17 Washington
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – A year ago, Keith Brown watched the Apple Cup in street clothes. He was out of action for last season’s game, as he was for the entire season, sitting out with a shoulder injury he sustained during fall camp.

It was a costly development for the Cougars and their defense, which could have used Brown’s veteran touch at linebacker, in the Apple Cup and beyond. Instead, he had his shoulder in a brace, recovering from the surgery he underwent before the season.

If Brown was itching to get back on the field, he showed it in one play, the best one the Cougars made on defense in a 24-10 loss to No. 17 Washington in Sunday’s Apple Cup: He helped stuff UW tailback Jayden Limar on a fourth-and-goal from the 1 right before halftime, greeting him just before the goal line, a critical stop for that group.

“We practiced it early in the week,” Brown said. “When you have a guy like Jirah (Leaupepetele) and Kaden Beatty in front of you, their job on that is to kinda just open the gap for me. So I was just ready to shoot it when they did. It’s kinda like a timing thing. We practiced it in the week, and it worked out exactly how we practiced.”

Take your pick on what you liked best about the way WSU played on defense in this one. The Cougars turned the Huskies over once on downs. They forced four punts, including two three-and-outs. They permitted just 10 points in the first three quarters, and games may not be won in three quarters, but it’s still an impressive feat for a WSU defensive outfit with lots of new pieces.

For WSU, it registered as a wholly encouraging outing on defense, which kept the team in the game for just about the whole way. The Cougars found themselves within one score in the fourth quarter on two separate occasions, which is far closer than the 24.5-point spread in this game suggested. Much of that credit belongs to WSU defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit.

Near the heart of that effort was Brown, who led the team with six total tackles, all of the solo variety. None may have been bigger than his stop at the goal line – a play that required so much individual strength and savvy from the Cougars that it paints a picture of what the unit could flourish into as this season unfolds – but it was his consistency and reliability that stood out most.

That mattered on Sunday, when the Cougars lost three turnovers, one fumble from running back Kirby Vorhees and two interceptions from quarterback Caden Pinnick, one of which came on a dropped pass in the fourth quarter. In those scenarios, Brown and his unit had to jog back onto the field at a moment’s notice, staring at bleak field position. They never looked worse for the wear.

“We just go out there, man. “Our defense is such a unique side of the ball. We don’t really care. I’m not staring at the scoreboard, staring at the minutes, you know? I’m just like, cool. Another opportunity to go out there and do what we’re supposed to do. No series is different than another for me, honestly. We just go out there ready to play.”

Keep this in mind, too: Defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk lived up to the billing. They had played so well in spring ball, had generated so much consistent pass rush in fall camp, that they figured to become one of the strengths of the unit. They played like it on Sunday, combining for nine quarterback pressures, five from McLain and four from Zunk.

They bothered UW quarterback Demond Williams Jr. so early in the game that as the rest of the contest unfolded, UW coach Jedd Fisch and the Huskies countered by getting the ball out quicker, running screen plays and quick passes for Williams. It’s a compliment to McLain and Zunk, the pass-rushing duo who figure to treat the Cougars’ future opponents similarly.

In fact, if there’s anything for WSU coach Kirby Moore and assistants to feel encouraged by from Sunday’s game, it’s their defense. They made a couple costly mistakes – missing a tackle on Williams and letting him convert a key third-and-long late in the fourth quarter will sting – but that’s to be expected against a team of the Huskies’ caliber.

The Cougars won’t get much of a reprieve next week, when WSU travels to take on Big 12 foe Kansas State. If Brown and the Cougs’ defense can engineer a defensive outing similar to the one they delivered here on Sunday, they could pry open the door to an upset.

“We already talked about it in the locker room,” Brown said. “We have 11 more opportunities, 11 more guaranteed opportunities to play. So let’s go out there and get better every single week. Let’s attack practice this week even harder. Work on the things that we didn’t do well and just continue to build off that.”

Washington State.title: WSU won’t face a defense like Washington’s again this season. But the Cougars have real concerns on offense | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – Somewhere deep within Husky Stadium, the site of Washington State’s 24-10 loss to Washington in Sunday’s Apple Cup, Caden Pinnick began to trail off. In front of a crimson backdrop, he was talking about his outing in the game, the touchdown and two interceptions he registered in his debut as the Cougars’ new quarterback, when he cut himself off.

He shook his head ever so slightly and said, “I’m just thinking about the 0-for-11 right now.”

That would be WSU’s conversion rate on third down for the entire game, a key reason why the Cougars couldn’t generate enough offense to take advantage of their defense’s heroics and climb back into this one. In their first eight drives, they lost two turnovers, totaled just north of 100 total yards of offense and, perhaps most importantly, did not convert a single third down.

That trend hovered over the Cougars’ entire outing on offense, derailing their best-laid plans. They did convert one fourth down, which led to Pinnick’s rushing touchdown in the fourth frame, but WSU will not feel good about this offensive showing. The Cougars lost three total turnovers, missed two field goals, tallied just 38 rushing yards from running backs, submitted two three-and-outs.

Before we get into the weeds on this WSU outing, the first for new head coach Kirby Moore, let’s explore a bit of context. First, it’s likely that for the rest of this season, the Cougars will not face a defense as good as the Huskies’. Washington’s defense, which returns 11 players who made starts from a 2025 outfit that finished No. 11 in total defense, projects to be one of the nation’s finest this fall. For that reason, many of the problems the Cougars faced here on Sunday – inside runs going nowhere, too much pressure on Pinnick, coverage sacks – may not be as prevalent in future games.

Plus, in the second quarter, WSU lost a key receiver to injury: veteran Tony Freeman. It’s unclear what exactly his injury was, but after the game, Moore called it “very unfortunate.” Freeman will get an MRI soon to diagnose the injury and provide a prognosis, Moore added. Freeman is expected to be one of the Cougars’ top receivers this season, if not their absolute best, so that kind of development surely threw a wrench into offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s blueprint and forced him to make adjustments that were never part of it.

Still, for WSU, that injury fits in with the other side of this: Lots of the things the Cougars put on display in this Apple Cup don’t figure to vanish as easily. Plenty of the other problems WSU faced will require fixing, not just putting Washington in the rearview mirror.

Some of the main ones center around playcalling. Perhaps the biggest error Miller and the Cougs made in that department came in the second quarter. Facing a critical third-and-5 near midfield, needing points on this drive to prevent things from getting away from them, the Cougars decided on a shotgun inside handoff for running back Kirby Vorhees. He gained one yard, and punter Max Dean sent it away one play later.

“There’s certain analytics,” Moore said about that play call. “Obviously, you get to a certain down and distance and you wanna be able to go for it on fourth down. We did not. We got 1 (yard). Was expecting hopefully to get a couple more there in that situation.”

On several other occasions, WSU showed a similarly vanilla approach to offense, trying to move bodies on the interior and run up the gut. Here are the yards the Cougars gained on runs up the middle by running backs: 6, minus 1, 3, 4 (fumble from Vorhees), 6, 1, 1, 0, 0, 8. That adds up to 10 carries for 28 yards, an average of 2.8 yards per try. It was clear from near the beginning of the game that the Cougars would not have much luck with that approach.

But throughout the game, Miller and WSU coaches kept at it, which registered as strange. The Cougars surely would like to be able to move linemen up front and run up the gut. But when you’re facing meaningful size and skill disadvantages in that department, it’s time to notice that and adjust accordingly, which didn’t always happen. It puts Miller at risk of making the same mistake that hampered Washington State’s offense for the first half of last season: miscasting players and, for lack of a better phrase, trying to force a round peg in a square hole.

The good news for Miller and the Cougars is that in the playcalling department, he wasn’t always so hard-headed. WSU unlocked some of its best offense when Pinnick rolled out of the pocket, when coaches schemed up space for him to take a second and scan the field, when they got their fastest players – Woods, Tank Hawkins – going to the outsides. They also got two sharp outings from receivers Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons, who combined for eight catches for 97 yards.

With those kinds of moves, Miller showed a deft hand and a keen sense of adjustments, which will be critical for the Cougs this fall.

“Those plays are definitely an in-game feeling. I think we got the ball rolling when we did that,” Pinnick said. “But I have no doubt that coach Miller is gonna put me in the best situation and seemed to be in the best situation to convert on some of these plays. We just gotta get better at some of these situational football plays, and we’ll be better.”

For WSU, the critical part will be this: In future games, in the two Power 4 tilts the Cougars have lined up in the next three weeks, can Miller be as quick to make adjustments? Or will he show the same type of conventional playcalling ideas, the standard dropbacks that resulted in Pinnick taking three sacks and scrambling countless other times from pressure?

“You gotta go back to first and second down first, and we gotta be more efficient,” Moore said. “We gotta create more explosives there on first and second down. And then third and long and XL, they’ve got a really good front, and sometimes that front was getting there a little bit quicker than we wanted it to. So that’s something we gotta look at.”

In Sunday’s game, WSU left guard Kyle Martin registered a Pro Football Focus overall offensive grade of 29.9, which is about 30 points below average. His run-blocking grade was 38.8, lowest on the team, and his pass-blocking grade was an unsightly 5.8, allowing one sack on four total pressures. He slogged through a forgettable game in his first career start at the college level.

But like several other patterns in Sunday’s game, across the rest of this season, Martin and WSU won’t face the same kinds of problems that the Huskies presented. The one key question: Can the Cougars make enough adjustments to avoid finding themselves in those types of situations to begin with? The answer may play an outsize role in how the rest of Moore’s debut season unfolds.

Washington State.title: Washington quarterback Demond Williams Jr. makes winning plays late | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
QB Demond Williams Jr.

The Huskies’ star junior signal-caller was mostly contained by WSU’s defense for much of three quarters, but Williams found a groove in the later stages of the game and made winning plays in the fourth quarter. He connected with Rashid Williams on a 44-yard flea-flicker pass to set up a short TD toss early in the period. With time winding down and UW holding a one-possession lead, Demond Williams made perhaps the play of the game on a third-and-9, eluding two defenders for a 21-yard gain before completing a 35-yard pass. UW went up by 14 points moments later to all but seal the game. Williams finished 24 of 35 for 268 yards and a TD, adding 61 yards on the ground and a first-half rushing TD.

LB Keith Brown

The Cougs’ senior defensive captain spearheaded a spirited effort from the unit, which kept WSU afloat while its offense struggled mightily to produce. Several other players in WSU’s defensive front could have been highlighted here, but we went with Brown, who made a number of strong tackles near the line of scrimmage during his first game since 2024 – he missed last year due to injury. Brown had arguably WSU’s best defensive play, stuffing UW running back Jayden Limar on a fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line to end the first half. Brown finished with a team-high six tackles, three resulting in gains of 3 yards or less.

Washington State.title: Washington State offense stumbles while defense impresses in Week 1 Apple Cup loss | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
The new-look Washington State football team, playing its first game under coach Kirby Moore, got a commendable effort from its defense, which kept the Cougars alive throughout the 118th Apple Cup. But WSU’s offense faltered for most of the day, allowing No. 17 Washington to control the lead all game and close out a 24-10 win Sunday afternoon at Husky Stadium.

The Huskies had chances to pull away earlier, but were hampered by their own missteps and a strong showing from WSU’s defense. The Week 1 Apple Cup between nonconference rivals was pretty sloppy overall, but it wasn’t uncompetitive.

New offense looks unsettled

Before the fourth quarter, WSU’s offense had advanced past midfield on just two possessions. The Huskies led 10-0 entering the final period, and it could have been much worse if not for WSU’s defensive performance and a mistake-prone Husky defense, which committed three penalties that extended WSU possessions – including a targeting penalty that negated a UW takeaway, allowing WSU to finish a fourth-quarter possession with a field goal.

The initial assessment for transfer WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick: not great. Though he was playing his first FBS game, against a talent-packed UW defense that put ample pressure on the sophomore, Pinnick often looked unsettled and perhaps relied too much on his legs. He completed 16 of 25 passes for 142 yards and two interceptions, rushing for 61 yards and a fourth-quarter touchdown.

As for WSU’s running backs, it was a rough start. Three WSU tailbacks combined for 38 yards on 16 carries, losing one fumble.

Other troubling stats for WSU’s offense: 0-for-11 on third downs, eight tackles for loss surrendered (three sacks), three turnovers and two missed field goals.

Adding to the rough Week 1 for WSU’s offense: Standout senior receiver Tony Freeman suffered a noncontact leg injury in the first half and spent the rest of the game on the sideline on crutches.

Encouraging takeaways for WSU’s offense: Pinnick is a good runner and showed some promise during the fourth quarter, leading two scoring drives; new receivers Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons had a few nice catches and combined for 97 yards on eight receptions.

New defense looks promising

A defensive unit with a first-year coordinator and a completely new lineup gave WSU fans plenty reason to feel encouraged.

The Cougs’ defensive front kept star Huskies quarterback Demond Williams Jr. off-balance for most of three quarters, getting significant pressure at times from potential star edge rushers Linus Zunk and Matyus McLain.

WSU gave up just one rush of 20-plus yards. But Williams started to find some space as the game wore on. The Cougars secondary may have tired out later in the game, allowing a few big passing plays after holding Williams to 108 passing yards in the first half.

The Cougs’ offense put the defense in some tough positions, committing two turnovers deep in WSU territory. One turnover resulted in a UW touchdown, but the Cougar defense held firm after the next giveaway, and the Huskies missed a field goal.

WSU’s top highlight from the game: The Cougars defense made a massive goal-line stand at the end of the first half, stuffing a fourth-and-goal run from the 1-yard line as time expired.

Throughout fall camp, it appeared defense would be WSU’s strength under new coordinator Trent Bray. Limiting an explosive Husky offense to 24 points to keep an upset bid alive until the late stages in Week 1 – that’s a good start for the group.

Opportunity missed, but the gap isn’t so wide

The so-called “competitive disadvantage” – the massive “talent gap” between a WSU program representing the new “Group of Six” version of the Pac-12 and a Husky team that now plays in the big-boy Big Ten – wasn’t so evident Sunday. The Cougs were projected to be routed, and even though they could hardly move the ball for three quarters, they were at the Huskies’ heels until the final minutes.

Yes, UW obviously has advantages in finances and talent acquisition and has advanced to the highest level of college football while WSU has been left behind. That doesn’t mean this series shouldn’t continue. In fact, two of the three nonconference Apple Cups have been more tightly contested than many in the later years of the old Pac-12. WSU beat UW two years ago, and last year’s affair was a one-possession game entering the fourth quarter before the Huskies pulled away for a lopsided win.

A win would have been a giant statement for the Cougs. It’s an opportunity missed, but it showed that WSU can still hang with the Huskies and there’s still meaning in the Apple Cup, which should be scheduled every year without question.

Washington State.title: Start of Kirby Moore era marred by uneven play, missed opportunities | TV take
Washington State.summary:
The Kirby Moore era started well. For one offensive play. Actually two. After that? It was up and down. Ultimately, though, as down as possible.

Why? Because the University of Washington earned a 24-10 win Sunday before 71,056 packed into Husky Stadium.

The first Apple Cup to open a season featured missed opportunities, missed field goals and missed calls – by everyone. Even, occasionally, by the trio that brought the game into our homes on NBC.

In the end, Paul Burmeister, Yogi Roth and Zora Stephenson performed more like Washington and delivered a winning effort in a game that dragged along until the final quarter.

What they saw

• Like the game, the broadcast trio started a bit slowly. Burmeister opened by calling the venue “ one of the best settings in all of college football.” That probably didn’t enthrall the hosts, who refer to their edifice on the banks of Lake Washington in advertisements as “the greatest setting in college football.”

And when the former Iowa quarterback referred to the Apple Cup as a game that features two teams “ ready for their most hated rival to kick off their season.” Cougar fans? Yep, they feel that way. Most Huskies? They see the school in Eugene filling that role.

• It got better though. Even if it seemed for most of the game Washington State’s offense reached its zenith in its first drive, one of two that ended in a long missed field goal.

Caden Pinnick, making his first start as a Cougar but his second in Husky Stadium, fooled the UW defense on the game’s first play, a 25-yard keeper down the sideline. The next play was an 11-yard dart to Daniel Blood.

The next 54 plays? A total of 206 yards. Much of it – 62 yards, culminated by Pinnick’s 11-yard keeper – came on the one touchdown drive, sandwiching the end of the third and beginning of the fourth quarters.

Then again, it’s not easy to win the Apple Cup when your offensive line is dominated by their defensive counterparts. As has been the case often in the past 15 years or so. Entering the final quarter, the Husky front had posted eight tackles for loss. Three sacks. Held the Cougs to 2.5 yards per carry.

Pinnick, who threw for just 50 yards when he led UC Davis into the stadium a year ago, more than doubled that with 142 – on 45 attempts. But he still was just 8-of-15 passing for 85 yards after three quarters.

So changes were made. The passing game got shorter. And the running game was all Pinnick.

“Again, it’s (offensive coordinator) Matt Miller saying we can’t really protect,” Roth said. “But can we get the ball out, nice job right there of finding a quick outlet to move the chains.”

And Pinnick took over.

“You’ve got to keep your eyes on Caden Pinnick,” Roth said as WSU drove in the fourth before Jack Stevens’ 42-yard field goal that cut the lead to seven. Smart. Pinnick accounted for 156 of WSU’s 242 yards.

• The Cougar defense was almost as good as UW’s. Almost. Though that shouldn’t be much of a surprise if you’ve been paying attention since practice began. The WSU defense dominated almost every day. And, except for a second-quarter Demond Williams Jr. run from 5 yards out, capping a drive that began at WSU’s 21 after Pinnick’s first of two interceptions, it did the same to the Huskies. Until three plays late.

“This defense is just impressive,” Roth said of the Cougars.

Pretty much. Until it needed to make one play to give the offense a chance. Third-and-9. Two minutes, 54 seconds left. UW at its 33. Williams has to scramble to escape pressure. Jeremiah Bernard hems him in at the 35. DJ Warner closes. So does Linus Zunk. All miss. Williams runs for 21 yards. Game over. Well, for sure two plays later, one a 35-yard pass to Chris Lawson and the other an 11-yard scoring run from Jayden Limar.

• The Huskies helped the Cougars stay in the game, despite Wazzu’s three turnovers. UW committed 12 penalties for 130 yards, including a fourth-quarter targeting call that survived a lengthy review. That call negated a fumble by Pinnick and a long UW return. And kept the Cougars’ second scoring drive alive.

What we saw

• Adding injury to the insult of a rivalry game loss is not unusual. But it rarely hurts as much, or seems as poignant, as what happened to Tony Freeman.

WSU’s senior wide receiver, who stayed loyal through the coaching changeover, seemed to stumble and fall on a first quarter pass route.

Freeman didn’t get up. Until he was helped by the Washington State medical staff. He went to the medical tent. Then the locker room. And then returned to the sidelines.

Where the NBC camera caught a touching scene.

It showed, from behind, Freeman standing to the right of long-time Cougar orthopedic surgeon Dr. Ed Tingstad, who once wore the same uniform. Freeman, supported by crutches and his right knee encased in ice, leaned toward Tingstad.

Tingstad reached out with his right arm and put it around Freeman just as the broadcast was cutting back to the game.

Freeman, called doubtful by sideline reporter Zora Stephenson, did not return.

• Speaking of Stephenson, she exhibited why such a position can be worthwhile as UW left the field at halftime.

Right after the Cougars’ goal-line stand, when Keith Brown and the defensive line stuffed the Huskies at the 1-yard line as time expired.

Stephenson asked about the play. UW coach Jedd Fisch, who NBC showed – more than once – throwing his headset after Brown’s bear hug, had an opportunity to share his thoughts.

“I’m not very happy about it,” Fisch said. “We had a half-a-yard to gain. If we can’t get a half-a-yard, we don’t deserve to get in the end zone.”

And what do they have to do in the second half?

“We gotta run the ball a lot better than we’re running the ball,” Fisch continued. “We gotta hit passes that we are not hitting. We gotta continue to play great defense but we gotta score some points. It’s embarrassing right now.”

How did the Huskies start the second half? By being flagged. With a delay-of-game penalty.

Roth offered the verbal equivalent of rolling his eyes.

Just like everyone watching most of the game.

Washington State.title: Early season Apple Cup makes for beautiful weather but ugly play | Dave Boling
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – Except for the beauty of a sunny day at an idyllic lakeside setting, it was a pretty grim afternoon. And for much of this unorthodox Apple Cup Sunday, it was fair to ask if this withering rivalry was even worth saving.

These teams were out of sync and obviously unpolished. It was a season opener, after all.

Washington State hadn’t yet learned how to score points, and Washington didn’t have an even rudimentary understanding of the rules of the game (12 penalties for 130 yards).

The effort was there on both sides, but it was a statistical nightmare of failed conversions and egregious infractions.

UW was less than convincing with a 10-0 lead at halftime, needing four red zone ventures to get that meager 10 points against an extremely determined Cougar defense that strengthened whenever backed to their goal line.

In the second half, Washington State made a game of it, and although falling 24-10, the Cougars made some important discoveries, particularly about their new quarterback Caden Pinnick – his arm, his legs, his sense of accountability, and, most of all, his toughness.

The defense will win games for this Cougar team under new coach Kirby Moore. Their bookend edge rushers will create night sweats for tackles in the new Pacific-12 Conference, and middle linebacker Keith Brown is the beating heart of the unit, making a goal-line tackle that would make every heroic Cougar defender over the years proud.

But the offense failed to convert a third down all day, going 0-for-11.

“Completely my fault,” Pinnick said.

Not really. Although, in the first half, he completed only four passes.

Pinnick found his rhythm in the second half, leading WSU on a pair of scoring drives, taking a fake-pitch trap play up the middle for an 11-yard touchdown to bring the Cougars back within three at 10-7.

The Cougars answered a UW touchdown with a field goal to close it to 17-10 with 4:30 in the game.

Husky quarterback Demond Williams showed why he earned his multimillion name, image and likeness status, while finally solving the stingy Cougar defense with a late scoring drive to take it to 24-10 – a far slimmer margin than the 22-point spread suggested.

Pinnick, a sophomore transfer from UC Davis, finished with 142 yards passing and 79 more rushing. His last-drive interception left him with a pair for the afternoon.

Washington’s defense is going to cause a lot of quarterbacks trouble this season.

It was on the Cougars’ fourth-quarter field goal drive that Pinnick most convincingly earned the confidence of his teammates.

Obviously getting more comfortable picking up yards on scrambles, Pinnick evaded a rush, speeding around the corner and up the right sideline. Husky safety Rylon Dillard-Allen torpedoed Pinnick – drawing the personal foul and targeting call.

The force of the hit caused a collective gasp.

Pinnick shook it off and finished the drive and the game.

Asked about it after the game, Pinnick shrugged.

“No, you take some hits (over) these years and you start to get used to it,” he said. “I wasn’t going to come out under any circumstances. I wasn’t going to quit on my guys.”

Pinnick said the Huskies showed some looks they hadn’t been expecting, which probably led to some of the third-down troubles.

“Hats off to them,” Pinnick said. “It was cool to see our team adapt around that. It was really promising being (within 3) at 10-7, knowing we were leaving a lot on the plate. There’s a lot to grow from.”

Fair assessment.

Moore pretty much echoed that when he met the press after his head-coaching debut.

The Cougs took longer to find their rhythm than he expected, Moore said. But he “embraced my role,” and was “very appreciative of the guys’ fight.”

The Cougars’ confidence, he said, didn’t have to waver a bit after this performance.

They were going to have to arrive at some solutions quickly, he said, traveling to Kansas State on a short week.

It would start as soon as they got on the plane. “We’re gonna have to evaluate the crud out of this tape.”

Yes, there will be some crud to get rid of, but there was plenty of tough defense and some burgeoning skills of a quarterback to brighten his evaluation.

Washington State.title: No. 17 Washington grinds out win over Washington State 24-10 in 118th Apple Cup | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE — The white-clad Washington State players surged to the sideline like bumblebees flooding out of a beehive, sending a hush of silence over Husky Stadium, which sounded mostly stunned by what had just unfolded on the field.

On the final play of the first half of Sunday’s Apple Cup, No. 17 Washington decided to go for it on fourth-and-goal from the 1. The Huskies handed the ball to running back Jayden Limar. He was greeted by WSU linebacker Keith Brown, whose teammates followed suit, stuffing him short of the goal line.

With that sequence, the Cougars created a tidal wave of momentum, surfing into halftime. The only question that remained: Could their offense take advantage?

WSU dropped a 24-10 decision in this season-opening Apple Cup in large part because the answer turned out to be shaky. The Cougars made things interesting in the fourth quarter on a rushing touchdown from quarterback Caden Pinnick, trimming the Huskies’ lead to three, but it wasn’t enough offense from WSU: Three turnovers, including two interceptions from Pinnick and one fumble from running back Kirby Vorhees, whose unit went 0-for-11 on third down and couldn’t enough momentum to cash in on their defense’s encouraging outing.

In Washington State coach Kirby Moore’s debut, the Cougars were undone by their offense, which totaled 242 total yards. Kicker Jack Stevens misfired on two field goals, which was an uncharacteristic development from the usually accurate kicker, missing two chances to get the Cougs back in the game.

Still, the Cougs clawed to within one score on two occasions in the fourth quarter, scoring all 10 points in that frame. One score came on an 11-yard scoring rush from Pinnick and the other came on a 42-yard field goal from Stevens, who connected at a key time for his team.

With that three-pointer, Washington’s lead diminished to 17-10. But the Huskies put the game away on the following drive, particularly on a third-and-9 conversion from quarterback Demond Williams Jr., who scrambled, made a couple defenders miss and jetted upfield. With only minutes remaining, UW had no issues creating more separation, scoring once again on an 11-yard rush from Limar to punctuate things.

Complicating things for WSU (0-1) was an early injury to starting wide receiver Tony Freeman, who went down in the second quarter, departed for the locker room and returned in warmup gear, out for the remainder of the game. It was a costly injury for the Cougars, who also rely on the veteran Freeman for kick and punt return duties.

For WSU, a few other wideouts helped pick up the slack. Transfer Daniel Blood enjoyed a sparkling day, collecting five catches for 57 yards, and fellow transfer Darrius Clemons added three receptions for 40 yards. Those receivers helped the Cougars move the chains at key times, including ahead of Pinnick’s touchdown, an 11-yard jaunt into the end zone.

With that score, which capped a nine-play and 62-yard drive, WSU pulled to within 10-7 — well within striking distance. But the Cougs’ defense, staunch throughout so much of Sunday’s game, followed by giving up a quick touchdown drive to the Huskies. Williams Jr., who completed 24 of 35 passes for 268 yards and two total touchdowns, hit a long flea-flicker pass to wideout Rashid Williams, who scored one play later on a pass from his quarterback.

With about six minutes left in the fourth frame, the Cougars breathed new life when Pinnick lost a fumble, but it was wiped out by a targeting penalty against UW defender Rylon Dillard-Allen. A few plays later, the Cougars turned things over to Stevens, who connected on a 42-yard field goal.

In his WSU debut, the UC Davis transfer Pinnick completed 16 of 25 passes for 142 yards, one rushing touchdown and two interceptions, one of which came on a tipped pass late in the fourth frame. He also turned in 14 carries for 61 yards, leading his team’s rushing effort.

Pinnick improved as the game went on — he hit on 12 of 16 passes for 103 yards in the second half — but because it took time for that to happen, the Cougars whiffed on several chances to make up ground early in the game. They went scoreless in their first eight drives, generating just 130 total yards in that span.

On WSU’s defense, it was a standout afternoon for the veteran linebacker Brown, who missed all of last season recovering from a shoulder injury. He followed that with six tackles on Sunday, none bigger than the goal-line stuff. Defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk also produced some real pass rush early in the game, setting the tone for the Cougs.

But it wasn’t enough for Washington State, which gets another tall task next weekend, this time on a short week. WSU returns to action on Saturday with a road test against Big 12 opponent Kansas State. That will be the Cougars’ second straight game against a Power 4 foe to open the season. To avoid two straight losses, they’ll have to generate more offense than they did here on Sunday afternoon.

BOX SCORE

First quarter

12:04 - WSU 0, UW 0: Jack Stevens’ 52-yard field goal attempt is no good after a promising drive by the Cougars stalls in Husky territory.

7:48 - WSU 0, UW 0: Washington uses its first timeout on the move to WSU’s 42.

3:53 - UW 3, WSU 0: Washington gets on the board after Tyler Robles makes a 48-yard field goal.

Penalties hamstrung Washington’s drive, which ended after 11 plays and 26 yards.

Second quarter

12:27 - UW 3, WSU 0: Caden Pinnick is intercepted by UW defender Jeron Jones after the ball was tipped.

UW takes over at WSU’s 21.

10:09 - UW 10, WSU 0: Demond Williams Jr. scrambles for a 5-yard touchdown.

10:05 - UW 10, WSU 0: Kirby Vorhees fumbles after a review overturns the call on the field.

Washington takes over at the WSU 23.

7:58 - UW 10, WSU 0: The turnover doesn’t damage WSU as Robles misses a 29-yard field goal attempt.

Halftime

Washington State enters the half with some momentum after stuffing Washington running back Jayden Limar at the goal line on fourth down.

Washington enters halftime ahead 10-0 in a defense-first Apple Cup so far.

The Cougars mustered 73 total yards in the first half, with quarterback Pinnick completed four passes for 39 yards.

Williams finishes the first half with 108 passing yards and 30 rushing yards to lead the Huskies.

Third quarter

6:59 - UW 10, WSU 0: Stevens misses a 32-yard field goal attempt. A delay of game penalty pushed the attempt back five yards.

0:31 - UW 10, WSU 0: Washington State’s defense forces a turnover on downs after UW drives to the Cougars’ 38.

Fourth quarter

10:15 - UW 10, WSU 7: Pinnick breaks free for an 11-yard rushing touchdown to get WSU on the board.

It was the Cougars’ most successful drive of the game, running nine plays for 62 yards and the score.

9:17 - UW 10, WSU 7: Washington responds quickly as Demond Williams finds Rashid Williams on a flea flicker for a 44-yard completion down to the WSU 2.

8:05 - UW 17, WSU 7: Demond Williams connects with Rashid Williams for a 1-yard touchdown pass.

6:14 - UW 17, WSU 7: Washington State dodges disaster as a fumble by Pinnick is nullified by a targeting penalty on the Huskies. WSU has the ball at UW’s 30.

4:30: UW 17, WSU 10: Stevens makes a 42-yard field goal to draw the Cougars within one possession.

2:18 - UW 24, WSU 10: Jayden Limar breaks off an 11-yard rushing touchdown.

1:48 - UW 24, WSU 10: Alex McLaughlin intercepts a passed tipped into the air by Vorhees to seal the win for the Huskies.

Pregame

Washington State begins its first season in the revamped Pac-12 against a bitter rival from the old iteration of the conference.

Washington enters the 118th Apple Cup ranked 17th in the country and boasts a 59-24 win in last year’s game in Pullman.

After the departure of head coach Jimmy Rogers to Iowa State and the graduation of starting quarterback Zevi Eckhaus, the Cougars turn to Prosser native Kirby Moore to command the program.

Moore brought in UC Davis transfer quarterback Caden Pinnick and mined the transfer portal for other impact players.

Washington State takes on UW at Husky Stadium in Seattle.

Series history

Washington holds a 74-33-6 advantage in the series history between the two rivals.

Most recently, the Huskies won last year in Pullman 59-24. Washington State’s last win came in 2024 after a dramatic goal-line stand at Lumen Field, 24-19.

Notable stat

Last season at UC Davis, Pinnick registered a Pro Football Focus passing grade of 87.1 against the blitz, which is a remarkable number.

Washington State.title: WSU's Ol' Crimson the first inductee into College GameDay's Hall of Fan
Washington State.summary:
Ol’ Crimson has been made a permanent fixture on ESPN’s “College GameDay” – even more than it already was.

Washington State’s flag, which has flown in the background of 338 consecutive episodes of the pregame show, was the inaugural inductee into Gameday’s “Hall of Fan” Saturday, celebrating the show’s 500th episode.

Ol’ Crimson’s streak began in 2003 in Austin, Texas, and has made stops all around the country – including the show’s first visit to Pullman for a game against No. 12 Oregon in 2018.

“And our inaugural inductee, somebody who has been with us for 23 years. They had a 15-year crusade to get this show to their campus, in the Palouse at Washington State. The inaugural inductee into the College Gameday Hall of Fan … Ol’ Crimson, the Washington State flag,” ESPN’s Reece Davis said.

The streak is kept alive by the Ol’ Crimson Booster Club, originally organized by Tom Pounds of Albuquerque, New Mexico, and expanded to fans across the country.

Will Johnson was this weekend’s flag waver in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He received a gold helmet and commemorative football from the GameDay crew during the broadcast.

Washington State.title: Two-minute drill: Washington State's keys to victory against No. 17 Washington in the Apple Cup
Washington State.summary:
Washington State at Washington

Sunday, 1 p.m.

Line: UW favored by 23½

TV: NBC Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU edges vs. UW OL: There may be no bigger matchup in Sunday’s game than this: How will WSU defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk fare against UW offensive tackles Kodi Greene and Drew Azzopardi?

Transfers from Idaho and Vanderbilt respectively, McLain and Zunk blossomed as one of the biggest stories to come out of WSU’s spring ball and fall camp, using their size and athleticism to generate consistent pass rush. But going up against your own teammates is not the same thing as facing Greene, a five-star true freshman, and Azzopardi, a fifth-year senior who will be playing his 33rd career college game.

If McLain and Zunk can produce meaningful pressure on Washington QB Demond Williams Jr., the Cougars defense has a much better chance of disrupting him and creating a turnover or two, perhaps shifting the tide of the game. If not, it could be a long day for WSU’s defense, no matter how sharp that group looked during fall camp.

How the Cougs win…

On defense, WSU’s game plan needs to involve consistent pressure on UW quarterback Demond Williams. On offense, the Cougars would do well to get their running game going, which does two things: It keeps the clock running and keeps the ball away from the Huskies’ potent offense. And it relieves some pressure off WSU QB Caden Pinnick, who endured a nightmare start last season at Husky Stadium playing for UC Davis, completing 8 of 16 passes for 50 yards, one touchdown and one interception.

Pinnick may have a far more talented supporting cast at WSU, but it’s a tall ask for a redshirt sophomore to walk into Husky Stadium and take down a talented UW defense. If the Cougars can get meaningful production from running backs Kirby Vorhees and Maxwell Woods – if their offensive line can create push up front – Pinnick won’t feel the pressure to make superstar plays and press early in the game.

How the Huskies win…

UW can win this game all kinds of ways, but the likeliest involves its defense, which gets a chance to give Pinnick an inauspicious welcome to his Cougar tenure. During fall camp, WSU’s offense had more than its fair share of shaky moments, and it’s possible the Cougars clean those up headed into Sunday’s game – but it’s no promising way to enter a game against a UW defense that brings back 11 players who made starts last fall.

In UW defensive coordinator Ryan Walters’ 4-2-5 scheme, linebacker trio Jacob Manu, Xe’ree Alexander and Zaydrius Rainey-Sale could vault into one of the nation’s premier linebacker units, with a splash of former Cougar Buddah Al-Uqdah sprinkled in. Pinnick will also have to keep an eye out for safety Alex McLaughlin, who picked off two passes in last year’s Apple Cup.

Key stat: 87.1

Last season at UC Davis, Pinnick registered a Pro Football Focus passing grade of 87.1 against the blitz, which is a remarkable number.

Pinnick will be tested against a UW defense which will likely bring

heavy pressure in the pocket

on Sunday.

Biggest question

Can the Cougs’ defense supply a turnover or two? As 24.5-point underdogs, WSU needs everything to fall into place to pull an upset in this game. For the Cougars, there may be no better way to swing things than to create a turnover, which could come from McLain or Zunk’s pressure on Williams.

Quotable

WSU DT Kaden Beatty: “I’m a Coug now, through and through. It’s in my blood. I bleed crimson and gray. So now, just having this rivalry is just something that I’m thrilled to be a part of. And now, I’m gonna be immersed in history with some of the other greats that have went through this building, these walls, and so I couldn’t be more excited and more fired up.”

Washington State.title: Why No. 17 Washington will beat Washington State in Apple Cup No. 118
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – Heading into Sunday’s Apple Cup, Washington State and coach Kirby Moore have said all the right things, have talked about all the right game plans.

The Cougars want to keep Husky quarterback Demond Williams contained in the pocket. Their defense wants to generate pressure on him and disrupt his rhythm. While Washington State’s offense wants QB Caden Pinnick to make the correct reads before the snap, and to diagnose the Huskies’ defensive schemes.

The Cougars have all the right things in mind. But as Moore said about containing Williams: “It’s way easier said than done.”

For that reason, we’re picking Washington to win the 118th Apple Cup No. 118 in relatively comfortable fashion, dispatching an upstart WSU club with a first-year head coach in Moore. The Huskies are just too talented, too deep, and too savvy to lose an Apple Cup at Husky Stadium for the first time since 2021.

For WSU, one of the bigger challenges will involve running the ball against UW’s defense, which is one way the Cougars could ease Pinnick into the game. The only problem for WSU is that many of the offensive linemen at the center of the operation, like center Noah Dunham and guards Kyle Martin and Nick Bakken, will be playing some of their first snaps of college football.

That’s no way to take down a Washington defense that returns 11 players who made starts on last season’s defense, which finished the regular season ranked No. 21 in total defense, including No. 11 in run defense. The Cougars might have a tough time generating a consistent ground attack, which puts more pressure on Pinnick, who is making his first start at the FBS level.

To be clear: For WSU, it’s OK to lose this game. It’s the Apple Cup, sure, and it means a little more to players and coaches and fans. But these programs are headed in two different directions – namely in terms of NIL budgets, which facilitates a widening talent gap – and the Cougars would have to play just about perfectly to pull this upset.

It’s probably best to reserve judgment on this WSU team until it gets out of the gauntlet to open this season, which includes three games against Power Four teams, two on the road. Drawing too many conclusions from Sunday’s game, unless the Cougars look absolutely uncompetitive, would be unwise.

Final score: UW 27, WSU 13

Washington State.title: The Apple Cup may be different, but here's why it still matters for Cougars and Huskies | Dave Boling
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – I’ve heard so much bellyaching about the irrelevance of Sunday’s game, this Washington State-Washington duel should be branded: The Crab-Apple Cup.

For instance, a comment heard from a sports fan/friend not affiliated with either institution engaged in this achingly non-traditional Apple Cup football clash at Husky Stadium on Sunday afternoon:

“Seems kind of meaningless, doesn’t it?”

Well, like so many things, it depends on your perspective.

I would argue that this game is one of the few things left in contemporary college sports that does have meaning beyond the dollar signs, and which, rarer still, continues to make sense.

Granted, it’s a pre-Labor Day, nonconference game early in an era in which the flawed business model of college sports – strangled by unsustainable operating deficits – has stripped teams of most recognizable affiliations and centuries-old rivalries.

That’s not to mention the negative effects on fan avidity when those rooting for the underdog WSU Cougars face the absurd reality that the quarterback of the opponents (Demond Williams, $4 million NIL deal) is making twice the salary of their head coach (Kirby Moore, $2 million).

And for the Huskies, well, the old team spirit might be questioned after Williams, in the offseason, announced an intended transfer-portal getaway, and re-opened the bidding for his services. He ended up staying, but it wasn’t out of his fervor to exert Husky Pride over the Cougars one more time.

Predecessors in these duels sometimes finished games with one side in tears and the other with roses between their teeth.

Now, with both teams being heavily manned by transient mercenaries, it’s hard to imagine a rivalry with less of the traditional bloodlust than this one.

It takes time to build up the required enmity to sustain a great rivalry, and such experiences are rare with revolving-door rosters.

Further adding to the frailty of this feud is that the current contract calls for just two more meetings after this one. So, the clock is ticking.

But it’s here for the time being. And that matters.

Especially for Washington State.

WSU has much more to win. UW has more to lose.

For the Cougars, it’s the debut of a new staff, in the initial steps of making its way in a newly reshaped conference.

No other team on the Cougars schedule is currently ranked in the Top 25. It makes this an early statement game that could be a huge springboard into WSU’s first fall in the new Pac-12.

Conversely, with a home defeat to a non-power conference foe in the season opener, the No. 17-ranked Huskies would be out of the polls entirely and already a step behind at least three Big Ten brethren ranked in the preseason top 10.

An upset road win in Moore’s head-coaching debut would be historic.

The Cougars went a meager 1-7 in Apple Cups in the revered Mike Leach era. And coach Mike Price won three of 14 of his Apple Cups.

As a native of Prosser, Moore has a life-long awareness of the relevance of the Apple Cup. He also served as a graduate assistant to coach Chris Petersen at Washington (2015-16, both UW wins). So, he didn’t just parachute into Pullman without a full understanding of the history.

Moore had been offensive coordinator at Missouri before taking over a position that had been briefly warmed by Jimmy Rogers, whose lone Cougar team lost 59-24 at home before Rogers decamped for Iowa State.

A year earlier, though, was the first of the nonconference Apple Cups.

Any WSU follower can still testify to the meaning of that game, when the Cougars held off UW with a dramatic goal-line-stand to secure a 24-19 upset at Lumen Field.

On the decisive play, the Cougar defense strung out an option run, with linebacker Kyle Thornton knifing through the line for a textbook tackle for a loss.

Thornton was the opposite of a transient mercenary, in his sixth season, becoming a team captain after having arrived at WSU as a walk-on.

It was perfection. Drama, significance, heroism, timing. It had everything.

Those are the kind of moments that make a game memorable, no matter when it’s played, or however many fans are crabbing about the absence of meaning.

Washington State.title: WSU, first-year coach Kirby Moore ready to try and pull massive upset on No. 17 Washington in 118th Apple Cup
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When Kaden Beatty thinks back to last season’s Apple Cup, when he ponders the way Washington used a blowout fourth quarter to bury Washington State and walk out of Gesa Field with the trophy in hand, he feels the sting come back like it happened yesterday.

In that game, Beatty played 24 snaps, still in a backup role at defensive tackle. Since then, though, much has changed: Beatty is now a starter. The Cougars are playing for a new head coach. The Pac-12 has been rebuilt.

And now WSU gets another crack at UW.

“I’ve lived with that now for an entire 365 days and some,” Beatty said. “So now we can go out and show who we really are and show that last year that wasn’t what we’re about.”

To knock off No. 17 Washington and win Apple Cup No. 118, set for 1 p.m. Sunday at Husky Stadium in Seattle, Beatty and the Cougars’ defense will have to follow through on that promise. WSU’s defense, the story of the team’s three-week fall camp back in August, gets the challenge of containing dual-threat UW quarterback Demond Williams Jr., who piled up five total touchdowns in last year’s game, showing off the arm talent and athleticism that makes him so dangerous.

Nine months after a wild saga – in which Williams signed a new revenue-sharing deal to return to Washington, change his mind and decide to hit the transfer portal, only to reverse course again and return to the Huskies – Williams is back to pilot a new-look UW offense. Gone are several playmakers who keyed Washington’s operation last season, including running back Jonah Coleman and wide receiver Denzel Boston (five total touchdowns in last year’s Apple Cup) and even running back Adam Mohammed, who made a surprise transfer to Cal over the offseason.

This year, WSU defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit will have to wrangle Williams and his new cadre of skill position players, including receivers Christian Moss, Rashid Williams and returner Dezmen Roebuck. The Huskies’ starting running back will be Quaid Carr, a superstar high school back who has yet to make a splash at the college level headed into his second season.

Still, before the Cougars can try to slow those players they’ll have to get to Williams, which is far easier said than done. That’s because he’s protected by what figures to be one of the Big Ten’s best offensive lines, which includes five-star freshman tackle Kodi Greene, returning freshman All-American John Mills and fifth-year senior tackle Drew Azzopardi, a staunch unit.

Can WSU defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, two of the brightest stars of the Cougars’ fall camp, generate enough pressure to bother Williams? That will be one of the top developments to watch as Sunday’s game unfolds.

“I just think we gotta do a good job of keeping him in the pocket,” WSU veteran linebacker Keith Brown said. “Don’t let him run free as much as he wants. He’s a good player, so I think as long as we can keep him in the pocket and make him throw the ball and throw the ball downfield, we’ll be in a good spot.”

“It’s a lot easier said than done,” WSU coach Kirby Moore added. “You look at containing the quarterback and making sure we’re sticky in coverage, and it really takes all 11 on defense. And then when you get in those positions, you gotta get him on the ground, and if it’s not the first guy, the second guy’s gotta be really close.”

On the other side, WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick gets his first start in the Cougar crimson and gray. It won’t be his first start at Husky Stadium, where he completed just 8 of 16 passes for 50 yards, one touchdown and one interception playing for UC Davis last fall. Can he improve on those numbers? Will he get enough protection from his offensive line, from tackles Ashton Tripp and Jonny Lester against the UW pass rush?

Washington’s starting edge rushers are set to be true freshman Ramzak Fruean and veteran Jacob Lane. If they can produce consistent pressure on Pinnick, it could force him into bad decisions, which surfaced several times during WSU’s fall camp. If not, he’ll have time to connect with receivers Tony Freeman, Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons, the Cougars’ starting trio.

“Really starts with command and operation,” Moore said of Pinnick, “the pre-snap, doing a really good job of communication with his teammates from play to play. The other team’s got really good players. They’re gonna make plays, making sure we’re picking guys up when that happens. We gotta be accurate. We gotta make great decisions. And then when scramble drill opportunities come up, he’s gotta do an excellent job of finding guys downfield or using his legs.”

No matter how this one plays out, this much is clear: WSU values this rivalry like it’s still a traditional Pac-12 game. The teams may be separated by conferences – Sunday’s Apple Cup will be the third nonconference installment – but the Cougars are treating it with the reverence it has commanded for more than a century.

Earlier this week, Moore said the rivalry “still means a ton for both sides and for this state.” In 2015-16, Moore worked as a graduate assistant for the Huskies, who back then were coached by Chris Petersen, who Moore considers one of his closest mentors. That’s one of a bevy of ties between these Cougars and the Huskies.

The one that has stuck in Beatty’s mind, however, is more about a bad taste. He’s let the memory of last season’s game drive him to make this year’s different.

“Winning the Apple Cup would mean absolutely everything,” Beatty said. “That is what makes this place go around here. If you’re wearing crimson and gray, this is why you watch on Saturdays – well now Sunday. Now we’re gonna see it on Sunday. It’s something that I’ve worked for all off season, something that I’ve definitely pinned on my calendar to look at and something that I’m excited for. So I’m just thrilled to be a part of it and to make history.”

Washington State.title: Explaining the Sunday Apple Cup, Fox's role in the Pac-12 implosion and more | Mailbag
Washington State.summary:
The Hotline mailbag publishes weekly. Send questions to wilnerhotline@bayareanewsgroup.com and include “mailbag” in the subject line. Or hit me on the social media platform X: @WilnerHotline. Some questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.

How did the Apple Cup come to be played on Sunday? How much choice did both teams have, especially Washington State as the visiting team (and it not being under the Pac-12 media contract)? – @draywilson29

The process wasn’t nearly as involved as you might think because both schools instantly recognized the opportunity.

Basically, the Big Ten floated the idea with the Huskies, who then asked the Cougars. Everyone was on board quickly. After all, the absence of competition in that TV window (Sunday at 1 p.m. on NBC) means millions of viewers will have their eyes on the teams. It’s a marketing dream for both teams and schools.

Washington State considered the competitive disadvantage that a Sunday game creates with a short week of preparation before their next game, at Kansas State. But athletic director Jon Haarlow told the Hotline a few weeks ago that “it was difficult to pass up the exposure. We want to get our athletes on the biggest stage possible.”

The Apple Cup is under contract for two more seasons and, in our view, should remain in this spot, on the Sunday of the Labor Day weekend, if at all possible.

Next year, the regular season starts in full force on what is now Week 0, so Labor Day weekend will become the window for everyone’s second game of the season.

That’s fine. Keep the Apple Cup right where it is. Sunday will remain open terrain until the NFL adds an 18th game and starts its season one week earlier.

I never understood how ESPN and Fox led the implosion of the Pac-12 and could not or would not find a seat at the table for Oregon State and Washington State. I know the answer is money, but how much will it take before the Power Four conferences break away permanently and leave the other 70 with table scraps? – Larry L

There is a fair amount to unpack here, but let’s start with this: ESPN and Fox made business decisions with the valuations of specific schools in the realignment game. Their role in who moved where was more passive than active. Conferences presented inventory options, and the networks responded with cash proposals.

The Pac-12’s implosion was the result of many things, but Fox was far more involved – first with USC and UCLA, then with Oregon and Washington – than ESPN.

Once everything went ka-BOOM, the networks were not about to pay the Big 12, for example, two or three times market value in order to make sure WSU and OSU had safe harbors. Again, it was business.

Moving forward, we agree with your premise at a broad level: Another rupture could be coming, but it won’t be the Power Four breaking away from the “other 70” (i.e., the Group of Six). It would be the SEC and Big Ten breaking away from the ACC and Big 12 (and everyone else).

What form that takes is anyone’s guess. It could be another round of expansion in which each of the Big Two add two, four or six teams.

Or it could be a super league with the top football brands leaving everyone else behind, including the second-tier schools in the SEC and Big Ten.

The system is deeply flawed – nowhere else in American business do two profitable subsidiaries pay for 16 money-losing subsidiaries – and it compels the schools to pursue every last dollar.

What are the bowl possibilities for the new Pac-12 teams? – Bruce C

The Hotline addressed this topic in detail last month before the lineup was made official and then in brief fashion earlier this week when the Pac-12 confirmed the news. But let’s offer a recap for anyone who missed our reporting.

Because there is some overlap between old and new Pac-12 teams, we’ll include the options for all 18 here.

For the bowl-eligible Pac-12 legacy teams not selected for the College Football Playoff, the lineup is familiar: Alamo, Las Vegas, Holiday, Sun, Poinsettia and Independence bowls (in that order).

For the six new Pac-12 teams not selected for the CFP, the ties-ins are to the Poinsettia and Hawaii bowls and what’s called the ESPN bowl pool, in which the network matches teams with openings across the games it operates.

One caveat: Washington State and Oregon State are only eligible for the new Pac-12 side of the Poinsettia, which is based in San Diego and making its return after a lengthy hiatus. The 10 departed schools will fill the other side of the Poinsettia matchup.

Lastly, keep the selection process in mind: For the Pac-12 legacy schools, the pecking order is determined by overall record – there’s no way to apply conference record when they are scattered across four leagues.

Hope that helps.

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey is now open to a 24-team playoff (dumb) if all qualifying schools play 10 games against Power Four opponents. I would imagine the threat of an anti-trust lawsuit from the Group of Six still protects their automatic bid to the CFP? – @NateJones2009

That’s how we see it.

The sport is flattening at the top at warp speed, with more teams in the Power Four capable of contending for the national title (hello, Indiana).

But up and down the food chain, the gaps are increasing: The SEC and Big Ten are pulling away from the ACC and Big 12, and the ACC and Big 12 are pulling away from the Group of Six.

The distance from top to bottom has grown exponentially in the era of NIL and the transfer portal, to the point that it’s difficult to envision a Group of Six team ever winning its opening-round match in the 12-team playoff.

That said, we agree with your premise: The threat of legal action will ensure the Group of Six retains an automatic bid to the 24-team playoff.

Some would argue that the Group of Six deserves two automatic bids. If it’s guaranteed one spot in the 12-team version, it should have two if the field doubles. That’s only fair, right?

Well, college football is no place for fairness and equity. If given the choice, the Big Ten and SEC would open the 24-team playoff to 24 at-large teams, rather than reserving one spot for the 70 schools in the Group of Six.

But their greed ends where lawsuits begin.

One spot will be secure in the expanded event. Anything else must be earned through the at-large pool.

What is the penalty/fine for schools that don’t abide by their bylaws and put ex-NFL players on their roster? And what will conferences do when one of their teams plays a Group of Six or FCS team that features an ex-NFL player? – @Jimmy0726

That depends on the outcome of LSU’s highly fluid legal fight against the SEC. To this point, the Tigers appear to be the only team planning to have former NFL training camp participants on their roster.

Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris were two of many players across multiple sports who received a preliminary injunction in Louisiana district court on Thursday. Whether they take the field for the Tigers on Saturday evening against Clemson remains to be seen.

The SEC has filed a federal lawsuit in Alabama that seeks to confirm its authority to penalize member schools for violating conference rules – for instance, rules against former NFL players returning to college.

If the SEC’s authority is confirmed after the Tigers put Wright and Harris on the field, the sanctions will be significant.

To this point, the other 15 SEC schools, plus the ACC, Big Ten, Big 12, Sun Belt, American and Mountain West have stated their opposition to rostering NFL players. (Notably, the Pac-12 has not, and its silence is becoming increasingly conspicuous.)

So we don’t expect other former NFL players to join rosters this season, but you never know.

Also, one reminder: This should be a one-time issue because the NCAA rule change that created the five-to-play-five policy only impacts members of the high school class of 2022, who were arbitrarily excluded. Players in the class of 2023 are eligible under the five-for-five ruling, so there won’t be cases like Wright and Harris next summer.

Previously, the Hotline identified the ACC exit cost at almost a billion dollars per school. Just exactly how did you calculate those numbers? – @JimSkin70758794

Honestly, I don’t remember publishing a specific cost for schools to exit the ACC prior to the expiration of the grant-of-rights in 2036, but it works in this fashion (for all schools) based on the negotiated settlement between the ACC and Clemson and Florida State:

• Any school that departs in the current fiscal year would owe a total of $1.1 billion, based on the annual exit payments compounding over 10 years.

• Starting in 2030, the annual fees drop to a flat rate of $75 million until 2036.

If the Seminoles, for example, left for the SEC in the fiscal year that begins next July, they would owe $930 million.

If they wait until the summer of 2030, the same year the Big Ten’s media rights deal expires, they would owe $450 million (or $75 million annually for six years).

That’s why the 2030 window is seen as a possible rupture point.

It won’t be cheap to leave for the SEC or Big Ten, but it would be cheap-er.

And there is zero doubt that if given the opportunity, Clemson, Florida State, Miami and North Carolina would find the money needed to make it work.

How about the Big Ten vs. the SEC and the ACC vs. the Big 12 in cross-conference football challenges? With a 24-team playoff field, why not play 10 conference games? Scheduling will follow the money. – Jon J

With the start of the regular season and all the controversy over former NFL players joining LSU’s team (more on that below), it was easy to miss a significant development on the scheduling front that happens to relate directly to College Football Playoff expansion.

It impacts every conference in both the Power Four and the Group of Six.

Here’s the important background:

• The SEC and ACC recently switched to nine-game conference schedules, joining the Big Ten and Big 12 in that regard. That means all 67 teams in the Power Four leagues have three spots available for non-conference games.

• The SEC, ACC and Big 12 have policies requiring their schools to play 10 total games against Power Four opponents: nine within league and one outside of league. The Big Ten has no such policy and, with a few exceptions, its non-conference schedules stink.

What happened this week? According to multiple media reports, SEC commissioner Greg Sankey has informed his peers on the CFP management committee that he would consider approving a 24-team playoff if the Big Ten requires its teams to play 10 Power Four games.

(The TV money also has to be right for playoff expansion. But clearly, the SEC cares about uniform scheduling policies.)

The Big Ten will almost certainly agree to the trade: It adds the 10-game requirement, and the SEC approves the 24-team field.

At that point, it’s easy to envision the next steps:

1. The Big Ten and SEC rekindle their discussions about an in-season crossover series that allows them to negotiate for more media rights revenue from their partners, Fox (Big Ten) and ESPN (SEC). The series might not include all 34 schools each year, but it would be designed to generate choice matchups with national appeal.

2. With the crossover series filling one of the three non-conference slots for each school, the Big Ten and SEC begin canceling whatever remaining matchups are under contract against ACC and Big 12 opponents. Why? Because they want to play cupcakes in the two remaining non-conference windows. (The exceptions here would be in-state rivalries like Clemson-South Carolina and Louisville-Kentucky. There are political reasons for those to continue.)

3. Seeing their options for quality non-conference matchups dwindle, the ACC and Big 12 respond with a crossover series of their own. That leaves each conference with the same plan (two cupcakes) for the remaining non-conference slots on their schedules.

4. Obviously, this is problematic for the Group of Six, especially the top programs. As a result, the Pac-12, American and others begin discussing crossover series at their level.

Within a few years, the nature of non-conference schedules changes dramatically.

To be clear, this outcome might not be inevitable. But in our view, it’s more likely than not (assuming the SEC and Big Ten agree on playoff expansion).

The Hotline has long been a proponent of the Big 12 moving to a 10-game conference schedule to increase the value of its total football inventory. But if the above scenario unfolds and a crossover series with the ACC becomes reality, the likelihood of 10 conference games diminishes.

We should have a better feel for the situation by the end of the year.

Sankey and Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti, who favors CFP expansion – one reason for his support is the benefits it would create for non-conference scheduling – are facing a Dec. 1 deadline to agree on expansion in time for the 2027 season.

Washington State.title: WSU TE Peyton Read to miss Apple Cup, DT Soni Finau's eligibility status still unclear | Notebook
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When Sunday’s Apple Cup arrives, Washington State will be at full health.

Almost.

The Cougars are likely to be without redshirt freshman Peyton Read, one of the team’s best pass-catching tight ends, who is dealing with what coach Kirby Moore called “a little nick.” Read missed the last couple of practices for WSU fall camp, which wrapped up in late August.

“He’ll be with us, but at the same time, he’s working through just a little nick,” Moore said.

WSU’s top two tight ends, likely starter Jack Pedersen and backup Beau Baker, are expected to be available.

During fall camp, Read emerged as a sharp tight end in the pass-catching department, particularly when Baker was out with an injury and Pedersen was out for rest and injury-prevention reasons. In the Cougars’ first of two fall camp scrimmages, he hauled in six catches for 31 yards, showing his reliable hands and shiftiness in the open field.

Still, it’s unclear how much he will see the field this season because Pedersen and Baker are ahead of him. A veteran transfer from UCLA, Pedersen is likely to start throughout this season, and Baker is ready for his redshirt sophomore season, his second with the Cougars.

In other roster news, Moore said Friday he has no update on the eligibility status of defensive tackle Soni Finau, who is attempting to rejoin the team thanks to the NCAA’s new 5-for-5 eligibility model. After playing one season with WSU last season, Finau ran out of eligibility, but a new NCAA ruling which gave extra eligibility to players from the high school class of 2022 allowed him to explore a return to the team.

WSU’s compliance office is working with Finau on his potential renewed eligibility, a team spokesman confirmed to The Spokesman-Review in mid-August. The sides have lots of details to work through, which is why Finau hasn’t been added to the team’s roster. The Cougars’ goal is to get Finau ready to return to play, but he will miss Week 1 at the very least.

“I’m still waiting from that standpoint of where things are at,” Moore said.

The good news for the Cougars is that defensive tackle is their deepest position. Their likely starters include Kaden Beatty and Paul Hutson III, with transfers like Jirah Leaupepetele, Damarjhe Lewis and Balaam Miller in line for meaningful roles off the bench. Add in WSU’s potent edge rusher duo of Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk and the Cougars’ defensive front looks like one of the team’s top strengths.

After playing the first three years of his career at FCS Cal Poly, Finau transferred to WSU for the 2025 season, making 3.5 sacks and 12 tackles in all 13 games. He played a backup role, which is likely the kind of gig he could earn on this WSU defensive line.
