Washington State.title: 'I wouldn't change a thing': To earn WSU's starting center job, Noah Dunham had to be patient — and ask for help
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – At first glance, you notice a lot about Noah Dunham, Washington State’s next starting center.

First, he’s massive, checking in at 6-foot-5 and a few pounds shy of 300. He’s also got two thigh tattoos, one with a black 1971 inscription and the other with 1975 lettering, the years that parents Andrea and Mike were born. You also notice that he smiles easily, much closer to a giant teddy bear than an intimidating Division-I football player.

What you don’t understand until you get to know him, though, is what has helped him finally earn a starting role after waiting three long years for the opportunity: He has no problem asking for help. Before a couple days of the Cougars’ fall camp, he says, he arrived at the Cougar Football Complex feeling a bit off, a bit sluggish. In those instances, he gave his teammates on the offensive line a heads up. “I’ve got no shame,” he says. “I’ll tell them, like, hey, I need y’all a little more today.”

In his fourth season at WSU, Dunham has transitioned from guard to center, making what would normally be a turbulent change seem seamless. He earned first-team reps across spring ball and fall camp, indicating that when WSU’s offense takes the field Sunday afternoon at No. 17 Washington in both teams’ season-openers, Dunham will be the one snapping the ball to Cougar quarterback Caden Pinnick.

To earn such an opportunity, Dunham had to show the patience of a monk. He redshirted and didn’t play as a true freshman in 2023. He played in just three games in 2024. Last season, he played in nine games, including two as a starter, but those appearances came because of injuries to WSU’s starters. Heading into this fall, Dunham has played fewer than 250 snaps of offense at the college level.

Somewhere near the heart of the operation has been Dunham’s combination of patience and willingness to ask for help, two qualities that some people spend their entire lives developing. At age 21, Dunham has gotten them down, which has paved the way to the biggest opportunity of his life: A starting role in coach Kirby Moore’s offense, a key gig on a Washington State team that figures to compete for the top half of the retooled Pac-12.

“I think it’s a little mix of both, of me being open and them just knowing me so well,” Dunham said. “They can tell when something’s off. So besides them knowing, they can tell I’m a little flat, I don’t know. It really is like brothers. It just feels like I’m talking to my family.”

“He just trusts his teammates, the guys next to him,” said Mike, Noah’s father. “He takes his responsibilities so seriously that it would hurt him to let them down, and if he knew that he was stepping into a battle and that he couldn’t perform to the level that the expectation is, he would be like, ‘I need someone to step in because I cannot do this.’ It would really bother him to let his teammates down. It’s a very humbling thing for him to do, but he would rather not let the team down than hurt himself.”

It’s a tricky thing: Dunham’s family, the teammates he calls brothers, have sometimes been the same men he’s competing against for jobs. How does he walk that fine line? If you aren’t sure, well, you might not know Noah Dunham.

• • •

Dunham knew he was close last year. During last season’s fall camp, he was locked in a position battle with transfer AJ Vaipulu for the starting right guard spot, which was the position Dunham played as a freshman. He’s always fashioned himself an interior offensive lineman – he briefly moved to center as a sophomore – and now with more experience in the program, he figured his time was coming soon.

After a weekslong competition, coaches awarded the starting spot to Vaipulu, making Dunham the backup. Dunham went on to play a shade over 200 snaps of offense that season – he made starts against Toledo and Oregon State when injuries befell the Cougs’ offensive line – but all told, it added up to another year of waiting for the Yuba City, California, native.

If Dunham felt any frustration, he didn’t show it. Instead, what he showed was quite the opposite: an inclination to learn, a sense of urgency to pick up things from Vaipulu’s game that would help him with his own. In practice, when Dunham would notice Vaipulu working on things that weren’t coming from coaches, he would go up to Vaipulu.

“And I’d go ask him about that,” Dunham said. “That was what I thought was really cool: we both knew it. We were fighting for that spot, but he had no problem helping me out. Whenever we talk ball, it wasn’t like he was to give me shortcuts so I mess up or anything. He’s telling me exactly what he does, to get me better, even though he knows that I’m on his heels.”

“As the mom, I was like, ‘I’m so mad about that. This is so unfair. This is so unfair,’” Andrea said. “And then the 20-year-old turns around, and he’s more mature than I am. He says, ‘no, mom, it’s OK. He won the battle fair and square, and it’s OK. It wasn’t in God’s plan for it to happen right now, and I’m just gonna watch him, and I’m gonna learn, and I’m gonna grow and develop from watching him and get better.’ And I’m like, ‘oh OK, fine then. Way to have that mindset.’”

Turns out, so much of Dunham’s patience and endurance comes from the way he thinks about things logically, the way he likes to examine how things are really playing out. When he was growing up, his parents said, his travel baseball coach would ask him series of questions like this: You’ve got a runner on third and first. There’s two outs. Guy hits the ball here. What are you gonna do as a defender? Where is the ball gonna go?”

Now playing center, Dunham has to think similarly when he breaks the huddle and heads to the line of scrimmage. In those moments, his eyes scan the opposing defense and go through a series of checks: He has to know where the tight end is, that way he knows which way the play is going. He looks to see whether the opposing safety is backed up or closer to the line of scrimmage, which gives him a clue as to what the linebackers might be doing, which in turn alerts him to more about what kind of look the defense will unveil.

He admits some of it felt overwhelming, especially in the first days of fall camp, when the Cougs were five or six new plays per day. But that’s when he likes to rely on more help, from coaches like offensive line coach Jack Abercrombie or tight ends coach Durham Cato. “They do a great job explaining to me,” Dunham said, “‘OK, if you see this, you see the numbers to this side, you know that it’s just defense.’ There’s only so much defense.”

“I told him the other night, he’s done a really good job with his physicality and his mentality, and that bleeds into the rest of the group,” Abercrombie said. “When he’s right with that, I know a lot of guys follow suit. Very similar to Ashton Tripp, which we talked about last week. He’s a steady Eddie, does the right thing, says the right things. Noah, naturally, playing the center position, you’re gonna be asked to do things, make the call, make sure everybody’s on the right page with the verbal combat in the pre-snap. Yeah, it’s critical. He has to talk. That comes with the job.”

That’s the other thing about Dunham: Naturally, he exudes a quiet brand of confidence, not the loud type. He doesn’t strike you as immediately talkative, and those who know him best say there’s some truth behind that. Andrea likes to joke that when Noah was a toddler, when the family would all be hanging out together in their living room, it would suddenly hit her: Crap, where’s Noah?

“And I’d just find him in the toy room, sitting with 100 books in front of him, sitting and reading quietly,” Andrea laughed.

Throughout Noah’s adolescence, he became a low-maintenance kid, the type who his parents never really worried about. He’s one of four siblings. He would never need a nap, Andrea said, and she knew her son would always fall asleep when he needed to at night. “Just the easiest, most quiet-natured kid,” Andrea said. “That’s kinda how he’s been all along.”

Liam, Noah’s older brother, is quite the opposite. He finds it easy to be vocal. Seeing that, Mike would sometimes tell Noah: “Noah, come on, speak up. You gotta lead with your voice.” Andrea would respond: “No, Mike, that’s just not how he leads.” Even at WSU, Noah has mentioned in previous years that he prefers to lead by example.

“But I do think that last season,” Andrea said, “towards the end of the season, when I mentioned that he started getting that fire in his belly a little bit, he shared with me that when his teammates weren’t doing what they were supposed to be doing, he was gonna start vocally holding them accountable.”

For Noah, that has been the other learning curve that has defined his journey, the new skill he’s had to polish just like his pass-blocking acumen. During fall camp, he said he had to work to “find his voice,” to feel comfortable speaking up and vocally pointing teammates in the right direction. It doesn’t occur to him naturally.

So how did Dunham unlock that level of comfortability? The answer is what ties his ascent together, the same reason he chose to stay at Washington State through the turbulence that has rocked the university at large: The Pac-12’s collapse and rebirth, two head coaching changes, hundreds of different teammates.

“The bottom line is just the connection part, getting to know people,” Dunham said. “I think that when you know someone on a level like that, they’re able to take your leadership role, or whatever you want to call it, more seriously. They’re not gonna look at me and be like, oh, he’s just talking. I truly do care about how you are on and off the field. It does get hard, and that’s what matters to me – how are you?”

“He’s resilient, hard worker,” said former WSU center Brock Dieu, who was teammates with Dunham from 2023-25. “He hasn’t always had it easy. He always showed up to practice and workouts with a smile, and man, he would work so hard. He would never take credit for the good things he did. So you can’t say enough. He’s a true offensive lineman.”

• • •

It’s quiet in the tight ends meeting room on the fourth floor of the Cougar Football Complex, which is where Dunham finds himself on a Thursday afternoon in late August, angling toward the end of his fourth fall camp at Washington State.

Just outside the room, the Gray W is bustling with athletes from an array of programs, soccer players and volleyball players and basketball players all lining up for mid-day grub. It’s a scorcher outside, so Dunham and the other Cougar athletes are grateful to have this facility, a five-floor complex that serves so many different purposes.

Dunham has been here before, at this stage of fall camp before. He’s gone through the hot practices, the slogs, the dog days when he felt like this opportunity was far away. Now it’s here. When he looks back, Dunham says, he appreciates the journey for exactly what it was: The long walk, the struggle, the route that forced him to confront his own insecurities and turn them into strengths, forging them into the kinds of assets that helped him transform from the long-haired freshman into the cleaner-cut junior at the — literal — center of the Cougars’ offense.

“If I was able to go back,” Dunham said, “I wouldn’t change a thing.”

Washington State.title: WSU hoops to meet Seattle U at Seattle Holiday Classic in December
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Chalk up another game on Washington State’s nonconference hoops schedule.

The Cougars will meet Seattle University on Dec. 19 at the Seattle Holiday Classic, according to a Monday news release, set for Climate Pledge Arena. It’s part of a doubleheader showcase, which will also pit University of Washington against Baylor.

“We’re looking forward to getting back to Seattle and bringing Cougar basketball to the thousands of WSU alumni in western Washington,” WSU coach David Riley said in the release. “I believe playing the other Division-I teams in the state is an important part of developing the game and honoring its history in the Pacific Northwest. We look forward to facing the Redhawks at Climate Pledge Arena and welcoming Coug fans to the Seattle Holiday Classic.”

It’ll be the third meeting in the last two seasons for WSU and Seattle U, which split last season’s series, then a West Coast Conference matchup. The Redhawks earned a 69-55 win in Seattle, and the Cougars followed with a 70-58 victory about a month later in Pullman.

It also represents another chance for each head coach to match wits. Riley and Seattle U coach Chris Victor were both assistant coaches at Eastern Washington from 2015-17. In fact, both head coaches ran the same first play during their first matchup last season in Seattle.

“The same exact first set, a Spain action,” Riley said after that game. “Just totally random. I thought it was funny. We worked together for a couple years at Eastern. He’s a great person. Every once in awhile, you can have some fun in these games.”

WSU’s next roster includes 13 newcomers: Mohamed Sankhe (France), East Texas A&M transfer forward Ronnie Harrison, Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (DII) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Sancho Moraga (Spain), Roman Stathis (Australia), Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele, Eastern Washington transfer wing Casey Jones (who was previously on a two-year church mission), Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and freshman forward Brayden Kyman.

Here is WSU’s known nonconference slate.

• At Washington (exh.), TBA.

• Vs. Davidson, TBA.

• Vs. Duke (Palm Springs), Nov. 21.

• Vs. Idaho, Nov. 27.

• At Murray State, Nov. 30.

• Vs. North Dakota State, Dec. 6.

• At Seattle U, Dec. 19

• Vs. EWU (Spokane), Dec. 22.

• At LSU, Dec. 28.

Washington State.title: Cougar Football Preseason Camp – Day 1
WSU lands commitment from French big man Mohamed Sankhe, rounding out next roster
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State has landed the final piece of its next men’s basketball roster.

The Cougars have officially landed French big man Mohamed Sankhe, he announced on social media on Thursday, becoming the final player on coach David Riley’s 2026-27 team. Listed at 6-foot-10, Sankhe is the mysterious post player Riley had been alluding to in news conferences since the spring.

Born in Senegal, Sankhe most recently played for Jean D’Arc Vichy Clermont Metropole in French Pro B, the second-tier pro hoops league in France. Across 41 games in the last international season, Sankhe averaged 5.3 points, 5.5 rebounds in 18 minutes per game, shooting an efficient 54% from the field.

More recently in this summer’s U20 Euro Championships, Sankhe averaged 10 points and 6.8 rebounds per game, turning in a similarly efficient field goal percentage of 56%, leading France to the semifinals. He scored in double-digits twice, including a double-double against Croatia (18 points, 11 rebounds) and an 11-point outing against Germany, including nine rebounds that game. He did not record any blocked shots in that span.

It’s unclear what kind of role Sankhe will play this upcoming season, but at the very least, he gives the Cougars some needed size. WSU has two traditional big men on the roster, including 6-foot-8 UNLV transfer Ladji Dembele and 6-foot-10 returner Dominik Robinson. They also have 6-foot-9 Northwestern transfer Tyler Kropp, but he’s expected to play the small forward or power forward spots for Riley’s team.

What the Cougs might have been lacking is a true big man, which came back to bite last season’s team, which often struggled to contain opposing big men with real size. That could be where they enjoy the presence of Sankhi, who collected four games with double-digit rebounds last international season, including one with 13 boards and another with 12. He figures to have little trouble hitting the glass for WSU.

Sankhe appears to be a true post player. Last international season, which included 41 games from September 2025 to this April, he did not attempt a single 3-pointer. In that way, he doesn’t fit the mold of a traditional Riley stretch big, but WSU does have a player like that in Dembele, who has shot 33% on 1.1 attempts from deep in his 70-game college career.

Can Sankhe be a true rim protector? That much is unclear. Last international season, Sankhe averaged just 0.4 blocks per game. That’s the kind of number you might expect from a guard, not a 6-foot-10 center. To his credit, he did record three games with two blocks, and he was playing fewer than 20 minutes per game. But Sankhe might have to become a more imposing rim defender for the Cougars to flourish on defense in his minutes.

Sankhe makes three international player’s on this WSU team, including Spanish freshman guard Pedro Sancha Moraga and Australia native Roman Stathis. Sankhe is also the 13th newcomer on the Cougars’ roster, joining a bevy of transfers from around the country that Riley used to restock a depleted roster from the offseason.

Those include East Texas A&M transfer forward Ronnie Harrison, Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (DII) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Moraga, Stathis, Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, Dembele, Eastern Washington transfer wing Casey Jones (who was previously on a two-year church mission), Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and freshman forward Brayden Kyman.
